# EU Reform Vision — Full Book

# Designing Our Retirement

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/designing-our-retirement

import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import KeyFigure from '../../../components/KeyFigure.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import PullQuote from '../../../components/PullQuote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';
import { default as T } from '../../../components/TermRef.astro';

{/* SPINE: a pension is a claim on somebody's labour, and the labour will not exist — so we shift our expectations onto machines, deliberately, while we still have thirty years of working economy. */}

Everyone talks about the demographic crisis. Nobody does anything about it.

That sentence is the reason this site exists. We have known the numbers for
thirty years. Birth rates across Europe are below replacement. The generation
now in its thirties will retire into a continent with far fewer workers than
pensioners. This is not a forecast that might not happen — it already happened,
in the maternity wards, decades ago. **The people who will not be working in
2056 were not born in 1996.**

And still the response is a shrug, a headline, and a return to quarterly
business.

<KeyFigure value="1.34" label="live births per woman in the EU in 2024; replacement is about 2.1, and the highest member state, Bulgaria, stood at 1.72" source="Eurostat, Fertility statistics" href="https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Fertility_statistics" />

## The thing that connects us

I was looking for a problem common to the whole Union. Not a Polish problem,
not a German one — something every member state has, whatever its politics.
The search had a practical motive. The Union is transforming, and it is
transforming toward the right and toward the national. I take that as given.
If we want to stay together through it — and from where I sit, in Poland,
staying together is the priority — we need something everyone can look at and
call sensible, regardless of how they vote.

Demographics is that thing. Fertility is below replacement in every member
state. It is the one condition we genuinely share, which makes it the strongest
available argument for acting together.

## What actually breaks

A pension is not a savings account. Whatever the paperwork says, it is a claim
on the work of people who are alive when you retire. Money buys nothing by
itself; it buys somebody's labour, or the output of somebody's machine. So the
question for 2056 is not whether the pension fund has enough zeros in it. The
question is: **who is going to do the work?**

Somebody has to care for an eighty-year-old. Somebody has to grow, move and
deliver food. Somebody has to run the water, the power, the waste, the buses.
When the working-age population shrinks and the dependent population grows,
those services do not merely get expensive — they stop being available. You
stand there with money and nobody comes.

<PullQuote>You stand there with money and nobody comes.</PullQuote>

That is the specific thing worth being afraid of. Not an abstraction about GDP:
a pension that buys nothing, because the system still assumes workers who no
longer exist — no one to care for us, no one to bring food.

## Two sources of work, and only two

If the work has to be done and there are not enough people, the labour can
come from exactly two places: **more people, or machines.** There will not be
enough people. The proposal is to shift our expectations onto robotics —
deliberately, as a strategy, not as a hope.

Europe's reflex has been the first source, and it is failing. It does not add
up economically: migrants arriving without the skills the economy needs cost
more in support than they contribute, and the highly skilled ones, who are
scarce, do not come here to wipe anyone's backside. It has not worked at scale
anywhere we can point to, and we would need it at scale. And there is
something degrading in the premise itself: planning to import people so they
can do the care work we will not do is not a policy anyone should be proud of.
What I would do instead — teach first, publish the criteria, then invite — is
[its own chapter](/book/education-and-migration).

<ObjectionList title="Three objections, answered where they belong">
  <Objection claim="You see robots because you are a programmer." verdict="Yes. Read what follows knowing that.">
    I should name my own bias. I am a programmer, so I see a nail everywhere,
    because I have a hammer. It is the one place on this site where I say it,
    and it applies to every chapter after this one.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Immigration is the answer, and Europe has always used it." verdict="Three parts, none of them comfortable.">
    Answered above in three sentences and at length in [Education and
    Migration](/book/education-and-migration), which is where I say what I would
    do instead.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Longevity dissolves the premise: if we rejuvenate, there is no labour problem." verdict="My bet is that the shortage arrives first — and the demand is the same either way.">
    It is possible that we will extend life significantly and rejuvenate. If
    that happens, there is probably no labour-force problem in the shape this
    chapter argues about. I do not know. Whether
    Europeans get access to that — to bioengineering, and to a long life of
    decent quality — depends on whether we organise ourselves so that it happens
    here. So the bet this site makes is that the shortage arrives before the
    cure does; and if the cure comes first, the thing we have to do to get it is
    the thing this site asks for anyway. The speculation is written out, and
    flagged as speculation, in [Redesigning the
    State](/book/redesigning-the-state#longevity-changes-the-equation).
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

## The case for machines

We are lucky in one specific way: the technology arrived in time. Robotics is
not a bet on something that might exist one day. Machines that move, sense and
manipulate the physical world — humanoid and otherwise — are being deployed
now, and the open question is no longer *whether*. It is whether Europe deploys
them at scale, and whether ordinary people see the benefit.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="Where the machines go, in the order they are ready"
  columns={[
    { label: "Municipal and communal services", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "Food production and delivery", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "Predictive medicine and healthcare", kind: "fact" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "What it covers", cells: ["Cleaning, maintenance, waste, basic logistics", "Autonomous farming and autonomous transport", "Catching what would become a hospitalisation"] },
    { dimension: "Why it comes first", cells: ["The most mechanical, the most staffed, the first to lose workers", "The most advanced civilian robotics we already have", "The cost that grows fastest as a population ages"] },
  ]}
  source="The author's ordering, dictated 2026-09-20; argued in Robotic Reindustrialisation"
/>

Said plainly, as a strategy a country could adopt: **we will automate as much
of old-age provision as we can, so that the few young people left are not
crushed carrying it.** Where the machines go first, and what is not machinery
at all — systems that let older people support each other, live together, work
if they want to, and stay connected — is argued in [Robotic
Reindustrialisation](/book/robotic-reindustrialisation#where-the-machines-go-first).

We are building the world we will retire into. That is a strange sentence to
write at thirty-five, and it is the most practical thing I know.

## Who pays for it

Two answers, and both turn the question around.

**We already pay.** Twenty-seven member states each fund their own
digitalisation, their own systems, their own procurement, their own mistakes.
Doing it once, together, is not a new budget. It is a less wasteful use of the
one we have.

**And we already saved.** Pension contributions are money set aside for exactly
this future. Part of it can be invested in building the robotics that will
serve that future — so that we *own* it, publicly, rather than renting it later
from whoever got there first — and so that it starts delivering public services
from the beginning rather than after some distant payoff.

**And daily life during the transition is paid for the way it is paid for
now.** Thirty years of living is paid from what was paid for earlier; nothing
about that changes. What changes is whether there is anything to buy at the end
of it. There will be, if we spent those thirty years building rather than
destroying, and if we built cheaply rather than expensively.

## Who ends up owning it

<T slug="who-captures-the-gains">Who captures the gains</T> decides whether any
of the above is worth doing: if automation replaces the labour our pensions
depend on and the returns go to a handful of owners, we have solved production
and destroyed the distribution that made solving it worthwhile. Ownership is
the second question, though, and models will be mixed; what matters more is
that the machines are <T slug="cheap-is-wealth">cheap</T> — affordable, open,
hard to monopolise.

<SideNote label="Argued in full">
  Why cheapness, not ownership, is the target: [Cheap Is
  Wealth](/book/cheap-is-wealth). Who the surplus has to reach, and the school
  meal as the worked example: [Who It Earns For](/book/who-it-earns-for).
</SideNote>

## The window

We are not old yet. We have roughly thirty years of functioning economy —
enough tax base, enough workers, enough industrial capacity — to build the
thing that will carry us once we have none of them. This is the last generation
that can pay for it. That is the urgency, and also the reason for optimism:
this is not a catastrophe we can only brace for. It is a construction project
with a deadline.

<KeyFigure qualifier="≈" value="30 years" label="of working economy left to build what carries us — the author's rough figure, not a projection" source="Paweł Żentała, dictation of 2026-09-20 (aging-society-frame.md:34-37)" />

<EvidenceBox>
  The claim that no national policy has reversed the birth rate is falsifiable:
  one member state back above replacement for a decade would do it. None is
  there today — the highest rate in the Union in 2024 was Bulgaria's [1.72](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Fertility_statistics).
  If one appears, this chapter's third step weakens and the site should say so.
</EvidenceBox>

<MeansForYou actions={["The next time someone says 'demographic crisis', ask the one question this chapter turns on: who is going to do the work in 2056? 'More people' is answered in Education and Migration; 'machines' is built in Robotic Reindustrialisation.", "Pick the layer you could build a piece of — the language, the digital state, the machines — and go to that chapter. The frame is only the roof."]}>
  If you are an engineer in Europe, you are not the audience for this argument;
  you are [the condition of it](/manifesto).
</MeansForYou>

# Redesigning the State

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/redesigning-the-state


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import PullQuote from '../../../components/PullQuote.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: systems expire, and whoever writes the design brief decides everything. */}

I had a dream once. We were flying through space on a ship, and we were the
fourth generation aboard. Our parents were around forty-two; we were
twenty-three, twenty-four. We were patching the ship. Pipes, mostly, with
two-part universal glue, the kind that is meant for everything, and grey
insulating tape. They leaked. The ship was breaking down around us, coming apart
while we watched. Parts rusting. A handrail came away and somebody fell.
Pressure escaping somewhere, constantly. It was hot, and we could not regulate
the temperature.

Here is the part of the dream that stayed with me. The people who designed that
ship designed it well. So well that the next two generations never had to
service it. One generation did not have to think about it at all, and only the
one after that started having any problems. But because it had been so good for
so long, the knowledge of how to tune the thing so it did not produce those
problems in the first place, how to maintain it, how to rebuild parts of it,
how to repair, did not survive. So the fourth generation could not cope. Glue
and tape were all they had.

It is a little like that with the European Union, and with every other
political system. A system goes out of date, because the times and the
circumstances it was built for have changed. But something else happens too:
the incentive systems get used up, or they get hacked. Everybody reaches the
finish line, and then something unsettling starts: corruption, elbowing in at
the trough. At some point competition disappears and what counts is the access
you inherited, handed down from one generation to the next.

That is when you have to restart the game. We are living in those times. We
will be restarting this game, and it is worth thinking hard about how to set it
up properly, so that the incentives are right for the generations after us, and
maybe even for us, if we happen to live a long time.

## The redesign is not a takeover

We need to redesign democracy so that it serves our interests: not so that
anyone dominates it in some bad way, but because there has to be a balance
between public servants and society, and the balance has to pay off. Good for
the people who want to work and get somewhere. Good for the people who want to
serve the state well; they should get something out of doing it well. A
motivating package, with benefits for citizens and for officials alike. The
state has to be thought through again, from the beginning.

This is not a generous afterthought. It is the whole mechanism. A system where
serving the public honestly is a worse deal than the alternatives will select
for people who take the alternatives, and no amount of complaining about their
character changes the arithmetic. Anything that only works for one of the two
sides is not a design; it is a fight, and fights get won back.

## Popularity contests, not contests of solutions

What counts in politics today is popularity. Popular views, you have to match
them, and that is how groups form: around popular opinions, or popular ways of
feeling. These are popularity contests. *I feel this way, you feel that way.*
There is no contest of solutions.

I am a positivist, so my question is a different one: how do you see this being
solved, so that both you and I end up satisfied? Where is the line, where is the
mechanism? How do we find the core, and build from the beginning, from values,
from what actually matters to us?

Those values are under threat now, perhaps even the European ones, from the
institutions that were supposed to guard them and from the people who work
inside them, who do not respect us and who trampled the fact that we are the
sovereign. So we start from values again. Democracy, for instance: where is it,
how do you build it. Not complaining, not shouting; doing the groundwork, and
the groundwork is designing a state. I think we can design one. I do not think
it is that hard, with artificial intelligence to help. The problem is simply
that almost nobody is working on it.

## Who designs the digital state

This is the thesis I hold most strongly in this chapter, and I would rather it
were argued against than ignored.

A **digital state** is the same system [The Total State](/book/the-total-state#why-a-digital-state-is-a-total-state)
describes from the other side: total in reach, and therefore potentially
totalitarian. Which makes it dangerous for officials to be the ones deciding
what it looks like and what its architecture is. They will build it so that
steering us is convenient for them, so that they can do it easily, along the
path of least resistance. That is not malice. It is normal. Everyone optimises
the energy they spend.

<PullQuote>
  The mistake is not theirs; the mistake is handing them the pen.
</PullQuote>

The nation's interest points the other way, and it is worth writing out as a
design brief rather than as a complaint.

<Callout kind="claim" label="The design brief">
  The political and digital system should extract the most value out of the
  state machine, not be the easiest thing to steer. It should force competition
  and advancement among those who govern, reward competence and good ideas,
  support European diversity while integrating, and leave room to experiment.
</Callout>

Every item on that list makes the system harder to operate from a console and
better at producing outcomes. That tension is the point. If a proposed
architecture is easy to run and produces little, somebody optimised for the
operator. Ask who wrote the brief.

## A shared core, your own deployment

There is one thing worth taking from China: their regions have a lot of
autonomy. They do not have a common digital state. I would build one.

Every country and region gets its own deployment, and decides how to customise
it. But the core, where we have an enormous amount in common, can simply be
shared. That way the whole European digital state works together, because we
are all running the same infrastructure. And European digital startups get
built on top of it, on European digital infrastructure. What that system would
look like is set out as a proposal in
[European eGovernment](/book/european-egovernment).

Then the part I find more interesting than the country layer. Ideally, digital
systems would be distributed where they are needed, rather than along
administrative borders.

| Kind of place | System |
|---|---|
| An old Italian hill village where you cannot drive a car; a Portuguese one; a town in Albania today | The same one, and possibly the best one for all three |
| A Scandinavian port city | A different one |
| Mountain tourist towns | Another |
| Industrial towns | Another again |

Different systems, deployed where they fit, built and shared in common. The same
goes for legal and administrative arrangements: they can differ between regions
according to the function the region performs. It does not always have to be
"this is one country, so here we do it this way". It can be more functional than
that.

## An offer to Germany

Now a proposal, and I want to label it clearly: this is my idea, not an agreed
plan, and nobody has been asked.

What the Germans built, that whole complex German administration, could be
carried into the digital world with its complexity intact, and I suspect it
would then be comparatively light. I think the Germans could take this on. At
least, it is what I would expect of them, and I think it is worth us expecting
it of them. Germany is a bit lost right now, and we should have expectations of
them. Offer a hand and say: listen, this is the role we would like you to play.
Europe is short of that kind of leadership. As it stands, it may be the United
States that says who leads, what Germany's role is, what we allow them. Germany
does not entirely know what to do with itself either. So give them an idea, one
they gain from and one we all gain from. Win–win.

{/* ASK-1 (redesigning-the-state-dump.md:119-128): the offer to Germany is published as you dictated it, labelled as your idea. It will read as Poland telling Germany its job. Keep it in this form? */}

I assume we would end up considerably more uniform than China, and customise
where we want to. Or perhaps not uniform at all, if the function-based picture
above turns out to be the better one. I do not know yet which way that goes.

## Longevity changes the equation

One more thing, and I flag it as speculation: I am guessing at a future, not
reporting a fact.

<EvidenceBox variant="against" title="The strongest case against this site's own premise, from its author">

It is possible we will significantly extend life, and rejuvenate. If that
happens, there probably is no labour-force problem at all in the shape we
currently argue about it: not if we can biologically rejuvenate and
bioengineering goes through a boom. The
[frame](/book/designing-our-retirement) this site stands on assumes no such
boom arrives in time; if one does, the argument about who will do the work
changes shape, and the argument about who holds the state does not.

</EvidenceBox>

{/* ASK-2 (redesigning-the-state-dump.md:59-67): R4 Q8. The passage stays, as speculation, with the one-sentence squaring above (editorial default). Keep it here, move it, or cut it? */}

Whether *we* get access to those benefits, to bioengineering and to a long life
of decent quality, depends on whether we organise ourselves, whether we arrange
Europe so that it happens here. We are the sovereign; we have to organise it.
Waiting for one party or another to do something does not work, and not because
parties are bad: because the system is set up this way. We have to change the
settings. We have to work out which system creates the right incentives for
those in power.

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "Treat the system as a design, not as weather. It was built by people, for conditions that have changed, with incentives that have been used up or gamed. What was designed can be redesigned.",
  "When somebody proposes a digital system, ask who wrote the brief. If the answer is the people who will operate it, expect a system that is convenient to operate and produces little.",
  "Ask for the solution, not the feeling: how do you see this being solved so that both of us come out satisfied? Most positions do not survive that question.",
]}>
  The ship in the dream did not fail because it was badly built. It failed
  because nobody kept the knowledge of how to run it. We are the fourth
  generation, and the glue and tape are not going to hold.
</MeansForYou>

<ProvenanceNote
  source="2026-09-25-redesigning-the-state-dump.md:21-141 (incentives, the spaceship dream, longevity, popularity contests, who designs the digital state, shared core and own deployment, Germany)"

# Education Instead of Import

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/education-and-migration


import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: decide openly who you are inviting, publish the standard, and do something about why they are leaving. */}

Importing labour will not carry an aging continent; machines will have to do
most of the work. That argument is in
[Designing Our Retirement](/book/designing-our-retirement) and it leaves a hole
people are right to point at. Saying "not this" is not a position. Europe will
still need people. Some of them will come from outside Europe, and they should.
The question is how we choose them, what we offer them, and what we owe the
places they leave.

This is not about closing a door. It is about deciding, in the open, who walks
through it, and about doing something for the people who never will.

## What our governments actually did

They took the lazy route, and then acted surprised.

Instead of teaching people where they already live, we moved them. We set up
incentives that selected for who could reach a border and endure the crossing,
rather than for who had prepared. We brought people into countries whose
language they did not speak, into labour markets that had no use for their
actual skills, with no published standard anyone could have worked toward. Then
we looked at the result, expensive, resented and bad for almost everyone
involved, and called it an unavoidable consequence of a complicated world.

It was not complicated. It was stupid. And I want to be precise about who I am
calling stupid, because this argument gets dirty fast: I mean the governments
that designed this, not the people who walked into it. Somebody who crosses a
desert for a chance at a wage is behaving rationally. The policy that made that
the entry exam is the thing that failed.

The failure is a design failure. If you never state your criteria, you still
have criteria; you just let geography, smugglers and luck pick for you.

## Teach first, then invite

Almost all of the alternative is available today over the internet.

Europe builds free online education for anyone in the world who wants it. Real
courses, in European working languages: English first, and German, French,
Polish and the rest where there is demand. Language teaching, vocational
training, and full remote degrees from European universities. Free at the point
of use, open to anybody with a connection. This should be our strategic idea
about work, not a side programme.

And alongside it, we publish the criteria. Plainly, on a page anyone can read:
this is the language level, this is the qualification, this is the demonstrated
skill. Meet them and you may come and work. Do not meet them and you may not,
and you will have known that from the beginning rather than after selling
everything you own.

| | Today | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| What selects | Reaching a border and surviving the crossing | Finishing a course and passing a published standard |
| What the person shows | Presence | A language, a qualification, a skill, demonstrated online |
| What we know on arrival | Almost nothing | What they learned, in which language, for which job |
| Who chose | Geography, smugglers, luck | The person, by putting in the work; the country, by publishing the bar |

That turns the whole thing around. The selection stops being *who got here* and
becomes *who put in the work*. You show that you learned the language. You show
you finished the school. You show you can do the job. Then we bring you over,
deliberately, knowing what we are getting, and so do you. We will need workers;
that is the premise of this site. I would rather we chose the capable and the
determined, openly, by a standard they could see, than take whoever arrives and
pretend it was a plan.

## The certificate is not a problem

A lot of people in the global south will enrol in a remote European university
mainly for the European piece of paper. I do not think that is an objection.

The education is real either way. A degree taken seriously enough to finish
leaves somebody more capable, whatever their first motive was. It helps lift
people out of poverty, with us or at home. And in many countries the remote
European course will simply be better than what is locally on offer, which means
our self-interested recruitment channel is also, without any extra effort, the
best schooling available to a lot of people who will never leave.

I am content with a system where the incentive that gets someone in the door is
a piece of paper, and the thing they walk out with is a skill.

## Taking responsibility instead of importing people

Now the larger part, and the one I care about most.

If we only build a pipeline for the ablest, we have creamed off exactly the
people a poor country needs and left everyone else where they were. So the
education programme has to be much bigger than recruitment, and it has to be
aimed at people staying put. Practical knowledge, free, translated by machine
into hundreds of languages. This is the thing that changed in the last few
years: translating a course into three hundred African languages used to be an
impossible budget. Now it is a technical task, and it is cheap for the reason
everything on this site is meant to be cheap:
[made once, used everywhere](/book/cheap-is-wealth).

| Course | Why it is on the list |
|---|---|
| Growing things: gardening, orchards, soil, what to plant and when | The first thing I would put online, in every language it can reach |
| Farming against desert: holding ground that is drying out, getting water to it | The places people leave are often the places that are drying |
| Wounds, health, basic medicine | What to do before a doctor, where there is often no doctor |
| Basic construction: shelter, sanitation, water, repair | The knowledge that keeps a village standing |
| How to organise: cooperatives, accounts, disputes, a decision a village will accept | Possibly with the same tools for self-organisation and [direct democracy](/book/direct-democracy#the-words-in-one-place) I want for us |

To stop global migration we have to start helping people where they are. Europe
has Africa next door: a continent with a young and growing population and, in
many places, nothing worth staying for. Perhaps we should take responsibility for
that Africa. Either we do, or we spend the next fifty years arguing about boats.

{/* ASK-1 (education-migration-workweek-dump.md:64-69): "wziąć odpowiedzialność za tę Afrykę" is kept as you said it. In English it can land as Europe telling Africa its business. Keep the wording, or add one sentence on what "responsibility" does and does not mean here? */}

Collecting what humanity knows about the practical business of living,
translating it into every language it can reach, and giving it away is the
cheapest serious thing Europe could do for the world. It happens to serve us
too, which is why it might actually get done.

## Bringing people here, and sending them back

The last piece is one people find uncomfortable, and it is the piece I am
surest about.

China sent its people to the United States to study and work, and then brought
them home. We should do the same thing, pointed the other way: this time we do
it for them. Educate people where they are. Bring them to Europe for a few years
to work and learn properly. And prepare them, while they are here, to go home
carrying something: capital, a qualification, contacts, the concrete experience
of how a functioning system runs.

That means the return is designed, not enforced as an afterthought. Some will
want to stay. Fine; we needed workers, that was the point. But the default
relationship should be an exchange, not a drain.

<ObjectionList title="The two objections I hear most">
  <Objection claim="You are creaming off the ablest and calling it aid." verdict="Fair against a pipeline. Not against a programme with a return path.">
    A recruitment channel alone would do exactly that. The answer is the size of
    the programme and its direction: most of it aimed at people who stay, and
    the people who come trained to go back with something. Without those two
    parts the objection stands.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="People will enrol for the paper, not the education." verdict="Yes, and it does not matter.">
    A course finished for the certificate still leaves a skill behind. The
    incentive can be the paper; the outcome is the person who can do the job.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

## An open door for Japan and Korea

Here is a case where Europe has the opposite problem. Not "how do we choose
among people who want to come", but "why are we making it hard for people we
should be actively inviting".

It is a scandal that we do not offer Japanese and Korean people easy access to
our labour market and an easy way to settle here. The Union should make that
simple and has not. They are exactly the people a country should want: creative,
hard-working, and often looking for a way out of a work culture that grinds them
down. It is a scandal that we make it hard for them. I would like Poland to be
the country that opens the door: work visas that are easy to get, a settlement
path a person can plan a life around, and on top of that the thing Canada does
under the name of a working holiday. Come, look around, take casual work or a
permanent job, and be told plainly that you are welcome.

We already have a thin version of this, which is the good news and also the
point.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="What exists, and what is proposed"
  columns={[
    { label: "Canada, International Experience Canada", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "Poland–Japan working holiday", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "Proposed here", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "Who", cells: ["Japanese citizens: Working Holiday. South Korean citizens: Working Holiday, Young Professionals, International Co-op", "Japanese citizens aged 18 to 30", "Japanese and Korean citizens, no age ceiling"] },
    { dimension: "How long", cells: ["Set per country agreement", "One year", "A year to look around, convertible into a residence permit"] },
    { dimension: "How many", cells: ["Set per country agreement", "500 visas a year", "Uncapped, or capped so high the cap is not the policy"] },
    { dimension: "What the work is", cells: ["Work permit under a youth mobility agreement", "Paid work of an additional character to the primary purpose, which is tourism", "The reason you came"] },
    { dimension: "Who decides", cells: ["Canada, by bilateral agreement", "Poland, by bilateral agreement (2015); a second with Korea (2018)", "Poland, by a citizens' vote"] },
  ]}
  source="Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, IEC eligibility page; Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy of Poland, working-holiday agreements and the Poland–Japan scheme page; both checked 25 September 2026"
/>

Canada's [International Experience Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/iec/eligibility.html)
admits Japanese citizens under Working Holiday and South Korean citizens under
all three of its categories. Poland signed a working-holiday agreement with
[Japan](https://archiwum.mrips.gov.pl/en/programmes/working-holiday-agreements/working-holiday-scheme-poland-japan/)
in 2015 and one with South Korea in 2018; they sit alongside six others on the
ministry's [list](https://www.gov.pl/web/family/working-holiday-agreements).
So the argument is not "we have nothing". It is that what we have is tiny and
kept that way: five hundred places a year, ages eighteen to thirty, one year,
and written so that the work is incidental to a holiday rather than the point of
the trip. A cultural-exchange gesture. Not a door.

Widen it. Raise or drop the cap. Lift the age ceiling. Let the work be the
reason you came. Make the year convertible into a residence permit for anyone
who found something worth staying for. None of this requires a new theory of
migration; it requires taking an instrument that already exists and stopping
being timid with it. And Poland could do most of it alone: admission rules are
largely national, and we signed the last two agreements without asking anyone's
permission.

<Callout kind="claim" label="A national decision">
  If there were direct democracy, this is one of the things I would bring to a
  vote, as my own proposal, in Poland. Every country can settle such things for
  itself, and I am against having them imposed on me. I will make the case and
  try to win the vote. That is the whole of my claim.
</Callout>

It is the same principle as the rest of this chapter. Decide openly who you are
inviting, say so out loud, and build the route. The alternative is not
neutrality; it is having no policy and then describing whatever happens as
though somebody chose it.

<EvidenceBox title="What would have to be established first">

The scheme rests on one claim: that somebody who learned the language and
finished a remote course integrates and performs better than somebody selected
the current way. That is testable. Run one cohort, follow it for five years,
publish what happened. Two smaller questions sit under it: whether machine
translation is good enough to teach wound care in a language with little written
material (one wrong instruction in medicine is worse than none), and what makes
a returnee's knowledge stick once they are back, which is the part with the
worst track record. Which language level and which qualifications, for which
jobs, is work for people who know the labour market, not for me.

</EvidenceBox>

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "If you can teach something practical, a trade, first aid, bookkeeping, it can be recorded, translated and given away this year, by you, without waiting for a European programme.",
  "If you work at a university, a remote track open to students outside Europe is an administrative decision, not a treaty.",
  "If you argue about migration in public, carry the constructive half: teach them, publish the standard, choose openly, and do something about the reason they are leaving.",
]}>
  Europe has spent twenty years with one side shouting *let them in* and the
  other *keep them out*, and hardly anyone saying the third thing.
</MeansForYou>

<ProvenanceNote
  source={[

    "2026-09-25-open-door-and-choosing-people-dump.md:10-28 (Japan and Korea; a national decision put to a vote)",
  ]}
  dictated={[

    "Clear, readable criteria for who may come; we will have educated people ready to work (:60-62)",

    "Take responsibility for Africa (:64-69)",

# One economy, one working language

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/one-working-language


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import KeyFigure from '../../../components/KeyFigure.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';
import TermRef from '../../../components/TermRef.astro';

{/* SPINE: English is the bottleneck of Europe's information economy; making it the working language of business and administration is a formality we already live by, and the fact that nobody has done it is the question. */}

So much is said about European integration, and nobody has introduced the language. Why not? It is only a formality. We already speak it: we do business with each other in English, we read each other in English, and making that official is not hard. Maybe somebody does not want integration to happen this way. Then it should be us, as citizens, who say that we do.

**English is the bottleneck of Europe's information economy.** A plausible reason no European startups and no European-scale corporations grew here is that we never had one working language. Europe's real failure is the absence of companies whose capital cannot be called French, German or Dutch, just European. Creating them is the point of language integration, not a side effect of it.

<Callout kind="demand" label="The ask">
  English as an official working language of European business and administration, in the interest of Europeans: not of capital, and not of interest groups tied to this or that nation.
</Callout>

This is the floor of <TermRef slug="the-three-layers">the three layers</TermRef>. The digital state, which is [the total state seen from the other side](/book/the-total-state), is built on the language, and the robots are built on the digital state; the order is not decoration, each level is what makes the next one possible.

## The scarce resource is the attention of the most capable people

A shrinking workforce has to be organised well, because there is no slack left. The scarce resource becomes the attention of the most capable people, and we already lose them to elsewhere. For them to work with each other inside Europe, they need a shared working language.

The same shortage explains why there is no European AI: no European science working shoulder to shoulder, and no shared language for it to work in. That argument is made in full in [European science](/book/european-science); here it is one consequence of the same missing floor.

<KeyFigure
  aside
  value="47%"
  label="of Europeans speak English as a foreign language; seven in ten of those aged 15–24 can hold a conversation in it"
  source="Special Eurobarometer, Europeans and their languages, fieldwork September–October 2023"
  href="https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_2686"
/>

What the reform looks like from where you stand, in the version first written down in 2024:

- wherever you are in the Union, you can speak to the local administration and complete its forms in English;
- contracts and court proceedings can be conducted in English anywhere in Europe;
- the Union's institutions produce documents in English that are legally recognised across member states, and the era of translating everything ends.

Language integration brings economies of scale on a scale few reforms can reach, and it is possibly the cheapest reform we could introduce. It is cheap because the expensive part, teaching a continent a second language, is already happening in every school; the reform is the right to use, in an office and in a court, what school already taught.

{/* ASK-2 (language.md:10-12, at git d2e092a): the 2024 draft asked for English as "a second official language in every EU member state"; the frame (aging-society-frame.md:64-65) and the 2026-09-25 dump (:153) say "official working language of business and administration". Is the ask still the full second-official-language status in each state, or the narrower working-language status? The chapter uses the narrower phrase until you say. */}

## There is no European public without a shared language

There is a second reason, and it is political rather than economic. **European political consciousness cannot exist without a shared language.** The awareness people build working together in business becomes, over time, the awareness they bring to European politics. Without it there is no European public, only national publics talking past each other.

That is why the ask includes media, not only forms: European media in English, because we already talk to each other in English anyway. A Union-wide argument cannot be had in twenty-four languages at once, and a Union that wants its citizens to decide things together, as [direct democracy](/book/direct-democracy) asks, needs a place where they can hear each other first.

## A shared interest is what keeps us from turning on each other

And there is a blunt third reason, older than the other two. A shared interest is what keeps us from turning on each other. The Union was built so there would be no more war; a common venture that stays worth more than any quarrel is how that works in this century.

Maybe we should have introduced English as the Union's official language after the crisis of 2008. Maybe we would be somewhere else today. Maybe we should have been building fast rail across Europe then too, while the workforce was still young, before we got old. We did not, and [the window](/book/designing-our-retirement) is now roughly thirty years.

## Where it starts: administration, including the military, and Central Europe first

The state that goes first builds its digital administration, its health service and its military on the language. That is the order: language first, then the whole digital state on top of it, then robotics, military and civilian. English official in administration means official in the ministries that matter most, and the army is one of them.

<SideNote label="Argued in full">
  Why one state, or a bloc, can adopt this without twenty-seven signatures: [Political path](/book/political-path#unanimity-is-not-needed-for-everything).
</SideNote>

Central Europe can go first. Deciding what language your own administration and your own business work in is an organisational decision, taken from below; it does not need anybody in Brussels to approve the idea of Europeans understanding each other. A group of states that already knows it is one bloc can do it together.

The research behind this chapter adds an argument the author did not make, and it is offered, not his. The armies of the region already plan, train and read their manuals with an alliance whose two official languages are English and French ([NATO](https://www.nato.int/en/work-with-us/careers/frequently-asked-questions)); an official English in the military would formalise what the alliance already runs on, and tie the region's deterrence to the language it is already conducted in.

{/* ASK-1 (direct-democracy-dump.md:153; chat 2026-09-22 in E006 PLAN; R4 contradiction 3): the demand in the dump is Union-wide ("język urzędowy Unii"); the path here starts with one state or with Central Europe, as in political-path.md:102-108. direct-democracy.md:193-194 says a state reforming alone is a target. Do the two sit together for language (Union-wide demand, regional start) or is the ask one of them? The section above assumes both. */}

<EvidenceBox variant="against" title="The strongest fact against this chapter">
  Almost half of Europeans speak English as a foreign language (47%, Special Eurobarometer, Europeans and their languages, fieldwork September–October 2023). The other half do not. An official working language that half the Union cannot use is, on the day it is adopted, the language of the mobile, the young and the educated; it becomes everyone's only as fast as the schools deliver it. The schools are delivering: [97.6% of lower-secondary pupils in the EU were learning English in 2024](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Foreign_language_learning_statistics) (Eurostat). Until that cohort is the workforce, the reform has a distributional edge, and a chapter that wants it has to say so.
</EvidenceBox>

<ObjectionList title="The objections, answered in five sentences each">
  <Objection claim="English is the language of a country that left. Ireland and Malta are too small to carry it." verdict="The precedent is on this side, not the other.">
    English stays an official and working language of the Union as long as Regulation No 1 lists it, and changing that list takes a unanimous Council; the Commission [said so after Brexit](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/languages_en). Ireland's constitution makes Irish the first official language and English the second ([Article 8](https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/cons/en/html)); Malta's makes Maltese the national language, both languages official, and lets the administration use either ([Article 5](https://legislation.mt/eli/const/eng)). Two member states already run the arrangement this chapter asks for: a national language, and English beside it in the office. That the language is now no large member's own is not a weakness; it is what makes it neutral in a way French or German can never be.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="France will never accept it." verdict="France keeps French. The veto covers Brussels, not Warsaw.">
    France's constitution says the language of the Republic is French ([Article 2](https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/en/constitution-of-4-october-1958)), and the [Toubon law of 1994](https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/loda/id/JORFTEXT000000349929/) requires French in public contracts and official documents. Nothing here asks France to change that: the proposal is an additional working language, not a replacement, and every member state keeps its own. At Union level France can block a change to Regulation No 1, because that vote is unanimous. That is exactly why the path runs through states adopting it from below, where no French vote is taken.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="It costs too much: teachers, translators, forms, courts." verdict="The expensive option is the current one.">
    The cost is mostly teaching, and the teaching is already paid for: nearly every lower-secondary pupil in the Union is learning English now. What the reform adds is the right to use what school taught. The cost of not doing it never appears in a budget line: twenty-seven translations of the same form, contracts renegotiated at each border, and the companies never founded because the founders could not hire across it. No figure is put on either side here, because there is no honest one to put.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="It is already the working language. Brussels drafts in English. Why legislate it?" verdict="Then it is a formality. Do the formality.">
    Brussels drafting in English is not a citizen in Poznań filing a form in English, a contract in Lisbon standing in court without a translation, or a Bulgarian engineer hired in Vienna without a language clause. What works by habit can be withdrawn by habit, and the people who benefit from the friction have no reason to remove it. If it is already the working language, making it official costs nothing. The fact that nobody has done it is the question worth asking.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

<EvidenceBox>
  Whether language is the bottleneck, or one of several beside fragmented capital markets, twenty-seven company laws and no single procurement market, this chapter does not settle; the author calls it a plausible reason, and that is the honest weight. What would settle it: a count of companies founded in the Union since 2008 that reached European scale, by the working language of their first hundred hires and the countries those hires came from, set against the same count for the United States. This chapter does not know of one.
</EvidenceBox>

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "If you run a company in Europe, make English the working language of its administration this year: contracts, internal documents, hiring. No law stops you, and every firm that does it makes the official version a formality.",
  "If you work in a public office, get one form published in English beside the national one. That is the whole reform at the scale of one office.",
  "If you are in Central Europe, argue for the regional version first: a bloc can adopt it without waiting for twenty-seven signatures."
]}>
  Nothing here needs permission to begin. A working common language waits for enough people to want it that wanting it becomes a fact politicians have to answer to.
</MeansForYou>

# European English: a proposal for a shared European standard

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/european-english


import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

## TLDR

English is already the most useful common second language in continental Europe. The practical opportunity is not to invent a new dialect, but to build a **European English Standard (EES)**: a shared layer for administration, education, science, business and cross-border public life.

EES would prefer clear and widely understood forms, document terminology decisions, test them with speakers from different EU language groups, and accept variation in accents and everyday speech. It would add capacity to Europe's multilingual system rather than replace national languages.

The first deliverable should be a tested 60-item vocabulary and usage pilot. Only after measuring frequency, comprehension and the cost of misunderstanding should the project scale to 200, then 2,000+ decisions.

## The proposal

The case for a working language, why English, why now and what it is for, is made in [One economy, one working language](/book/one-working-language). This chapter assumes it and asks only how a standard would be built. The original idea was a European English council able to settle questions such as `chips` or `fries`; the sections below turn that into a buildable proposal.

<ProvenanceNote
  source="book/language.md:12 (his 2024-06-22 draft, deleted in E006-T15; text at git d2e092a); the argument itself: /book/one-working-language"
  dictated="A council for European English that settles questions such as chips or fries; English as an additional official language in every member state."
  added={["The European English Standard, its decisions, phases, scaling plan, 60-item pilot and governance: research, proposed, not adopted", "Eurobarometer, Eurostat, EU language policy, Style Guide and ELF sources (sourced)"]}
  open="ASK-2 in /book/one-working-language (second official language, or working language of administration and business)"
/>

The council should not decide which accent is correct. It should maintain a **public interoperability standard** for situations in which Europeans with different first languages need to understand one another:

- public forms, notices and digital government interfaces;
- cross-border contracts, procurement and company operations;
- European research, education and media;
- travel, emergency information and consumer products;
- political communication between European institutions and citizens.

The national language remains the primary language of each country. EES is an additional shared capability and a common drafting target where an EU-wide audience matters.

## Why this is plausible

The 2024 Eurobarometer reported that 47% of Europeans speak English as a foreign language and that seven in ten young Europeans can hold a conversation in it ([European Commission, Europeans and their languages](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_2686)); 97.6% of lower-secondary pupils in the EU were learning English in 2024 ([Eurostat](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Foreign_language_learning_statistics)). English is therefore the strongest candidate for a shared operational language, even though proficiency and access remain uneven.

English is still one of the EU's 24 official and working languages, including after the United Kingdom left the Union. The EU already has language rules, professional translation services and IATE, its shared terminology database. EES would build on that infrastructure. [EU language policy](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/languages_en), [IATE](https://iate.europa.eu/home)

The European Commission's English Style Guide offers a useful precedent: it combines a consistent institutional convention with a strong preference for clear, reader-friendly writing. It explicitly distinguishes EU-specific terminology from the idea that the EU speaks a separate natural language. [European Commission English Style Guide](https://commission.europa.eu/system/files/2023-11/styleguide_english_dgt_en.pdf)

Research on English as a Lingua Franca describes European accents, grammatical transfer and mainland-European vocabulary as normal features of multilingual communication. It suggests that successful interaction and accommodation matter more than imitating a native speaker. [Modiano, 2024](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/weng.12646)

## Architectural decisions

These are the decisions to take before building the system. They are the research behind the proposal, not a position the author has adopted.

| Decision | Proposal | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1. What is being built? | A standard and resource system, not a new dialect. | A dialect cannot be legislated into existence; a shared drafting standard can. |
| 2. What is the default? | Plain, contemporary international English. | It reduces translation, teaching and comprehension costs. |
| 3. Who owns it? | An independent European English Board connected to EU language services and IATE. | The system needs legitimacy, continuity and terminology expertise. |
| 4. What does the Board regulate? | Recommendations, terminology, style, tests and versioned decisions. | It should guide usage without policing identity or accent. |
| 5. What does it not regulate? | Native-language varieties, accents, informal speech or literary style. | Variation is an asset and cannot be removed by decree. |
| 6. How are decisions made? | Evidence first: corpus frequency, comprehension testing and risk assessment. | The most frequent form is not always the safest form. |
| 7. How are conflicts resolved? | Prefer a transparent compound when a short word is ambiguous: `potato crisps`, `public holiday`. | Explicit meaning beats symbolic victory in a BrE/AmE dispute. |
| 8. How is law handled? | Separate `EES Plain`, `EES Legal`, `EES Technical` and `EES Spoken` profiles. | One register cannot serve a menu, a statute and a scientific paper. |
| 9. How is change handled? | Every decision has evidence, confidence, owner, date and review date. | Language changes; the standard must be reversible. |
| 10. How is fairness handled? | Publish uncertainty and country-level results; do not treat native-speaker intuition as the sole authority. | The users of EES are predominantly multilingual Europeans. |

## How it would be tested

### Phase 0 — define the target

Write a one-page specification: audience, domains, risk levels and what “easy” means. “Popular in Europe” is not precise enough. For each item, distinguish:

- frequency in EU institutional writing;
- frequency in everyday communication;
- comprehension without context;
- ability to paraphrase or explain the term;
- consequences of misunderstanding.

### Phase 1 — the 60-item pilot

Use the initial 60 decisions as hypotheses, not conclusions. Recruit at least five participants from each of twelve EU countries, balanced across major language families and age groups. Include competent non-native speakers, not only English teachers or linguists.

Give participants four tasks:

1. choose the meaning of a word or phrase shown without context;
2. select the clearest option for a public notice;
3. paraphrase the chosen expression in their own language or in English;
4. repeat the comprehension task after 24 hours.

Record `frequency`, `comprehensibility`, `risk`, confidence and country. A decision is a strong EES candidate when it is sufficiently common, broadly understood and low-risk. If no short word wins, recommend an explicit compound.

### Phase 2 — corpus validation

Compare the pilot answers with four types of data: EUR-Lex and DGT Translation Memory for legal language; IATE for EU terminology; ELF/VOICE-style spoken interaction for multilingual conversations; and consumer-facing text from at least ten continental EU countries. Report results by country and genre. An EU institutional corpus is not a proxy for ordinary speech.

### Phase 3 — live prototypes

Test the draft standard in three real products: a bilingual public-service form, a travel or emergency notice, and a cross-border business workflow. Measure task completion, clarification requests, time to comprehension and serious misunderstandings. A good standard should make people complete tasks faster, not merely make editors feel that the prose looks tidy.

## Scaling plan

| Scale | Output | Gate to continue |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | Pilot vocabulary, false friends and writing rules | At least one measurable comprehension result per card. |
| 200 | `EES-0.1` with domain labels and examples | Repeated evidence across countries and genres. |
| 500 | Public beta dictionary and style guide | External review by linguists, translators and practitioners. |
| 2,000+ | Terminology graph linked to IATE, EUR-Lex and translation memory | Versioning, governance, appeal and update process in operation. |
| Continuous | New proposals, usage reports and periodic revisions | No silent changes; every decision remains auditable. |

The data model should be simple enough to maintain:

```text
entry
  concept
  preferred_form
  allowed_variants
  avoid_forms
  domain
  examples
  evidence[]
  comprehension_score
  risk_level
  confidence
  version
  review_date
```

## The first decision set

The pilot recommends `fries` for fried potato strips and `potato crisps` for the packaged snack. It prefers forms such as `elevator`, `apartment`, `mobile phone`, `postcode`, `pharmacy`, `football`, `petrol`, `motorway`, `autumn`, `film` and `CV`, while allowing regional variants when context is safe.

It avoids false friends and opaque calques: `actual` should not mean “current”; `eventually` should not mean “possibly”; `make a control` should become `carry out a check`; `advices` and `informations` should remain `advice` and `information`. It prefers `will` over unnecessary `shall`, active voice where possible, explicit dates such as `27 August 2026`, and short sentences.

<details>
<summary>Open the full 60-item pilot table</summary>

The detailed table is retained as a research instrument. `P` means prefer, `D` allow as a variant, `A` avoid, and `U` use an explicit compound.

| # | Item | EES hypothesis | Decision |
|---:|---|---|:---:|
| 1 | chips / fries | `fries`; snack `potato crisps` | U |
| 2 | lift / elevator | `elevator` | P |
| 3 | flat / apartment | `apartment` | P |
| 4 | queue / line | `queue` in transport, `line` generally | D |
| 5 | holiday / vacation | `holiday`; `public holiday` for a state holiday | P |
| 6 | timetable / schedule | `schedule` | P |
| 7 | return / round-trip ticket | `return ticket` | P |
| 8 | mobile / cell phone | `mobile phone` | P |
| 9 | postcode / ZIP code | `postcode` | P |
| 10 | chemist / drugstore | `pharmacy` | P |
| 11 | trousers / pants | `trousers` unless context is unambiguous | P |
| 12 | trainers / sneakers | `sports shoes` in instructions | U |
| 13 | football / soccer | `football` | P |
| 14 | biscuit / cookie | `biscuit`; `cookie` for a specific product | D |
| 15 | sweets / candy | `sweets`; technical `confectionery` | P |
| 16 | aubergine / eggplant | `aubergine` in EU contexts | D |
| 17 | courgette / zucchini | `courgette` in EU contexts | D |
| 18 | petrol / gasoline | `petrol`; general `fuel` | P |
| 19 | lorry / truck | `truck` | P |
| 20 | boot / trunk | `boot`; `luggage compartment` in instructions | U |
| 21 | bonnet / hood | `engine hood` | U |
| 22 | motorway / freeway | `motorway` | P |
| 23 | pavement / sidewalk | state explicitly that it means a footpath | U |
| 24 | autumn / fall | `autumn` | P |
| 25 | torch / flashlight | `torch`; `flashlight` allowed | D |
| 26 | nappy / diaper | `baby diaper` in instructions | U |
| 27 | film / movie | `film` | P |
| 28 | programme / program | `programme`; software `program` | P |
| 29 | maths / math | formal `mathematics` | P |
| 30 | actual | `current`, `present` or `real` | A |
| 31 | eventually | `possibly` or `if necessary` | A |
| 32 | control | `check`, `inspection` or `monitoring` | A |
| 33 | make a control | `carry out a check` | A |
| 34 | sensible / sensitive | preserve the standard meanings | P |
| 35 | assist | `help` in plain text | P |
| 36 | participate in | `take part in` in plain text | P |
| 37 | implement | `implement`; plain `put in place` | D |
| 38 | competence / competency | `competence` in EU contexts | P |
| 39 | transposition | `implementation in national law` for citizens | D |
| 40 | advices / informations | `advice`, `information` | P |
| 41 | feedbacks | `feedback` | P |
| 42 | demands | `requests` or `requirements` where neutral | P |
| 43 | realise / achieve | `realise` = understand; `achieve` = attain | P |
| 44 | chef / chief | preserve the distinct meanings | P |
| 45 | agenda / programme | agenda = topics; programme = wider plan | P |
| 46 | library / bookshop | preserve the distinct meanings | P |
| 47 | resume / résumé | `CV` in Europe; `resume` = restart | P |
| 48 | precise / accurate | precise = detailed; accurate = correct | P |
| 49 | in the framework of | `under`, `within`, `as part of` | P |
| 50 | competence vs competency | use `competence` in EU language | P |
| 51 | shall / will | `will`; `shall` only for a legal function | P |
| 52 | must / should | must = obligation; should = recommendation | P |
| 53 | passive voice | active voice when the actor is known | P |
| 54 | nominalisation | `investigate`, not `conduct an investigation` | P |
| 55 | idioms | avoid idioms and culture-bound jokes | P |
| 56 | phrasal verbs | prefer an explicit verb in high-risk text | P |
| 57 | sentence length | usually 15–20 words in public notices | P |
| 58 | date format | `27 August 2026` | P |
| 59 | decimal separator | English `12.5`; document data conventions | P |
| 60 | percentage | `12% of respondents` | P |

</details>

## Governance and safeguards

The European English Board should publish a dictionary, style guide, terminology graph, evidence register, consultation process and changelog. It should include EU translators, lawyer-linguists, teachers, accessibility specialists, domain experts and users from different language communities.

It should not impose one national accent, treat native-speaker intuition as the only authority, confuse EU institutional frequency with everyday frequency, or use language integration to remove national languages. The political promise is **enhancing, not replacing** linguistic diversity.

## First concrete actions

1. Approve the EES charter: scope, principles and safeguards.
2. Convert the 60-item table into a small open dataset with evidence fields.
3. Recruit the pilot panel and run the comprehension tests.
4. Compare results with EU corpora and IATE.
5. Publish `EES-0.1` with confidence scores and unresolved items.
6. Test it in one public form, one travel notice and one business workflow.
7. Decide whether the evidence supports scaling to 200 items.

## Related

- [One economy, one working language](/book/one-working-language): the argument this standard serves.
- [The language layer](/vision#language) in the frame.

# The Total State

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/the-total-state


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import Playbook from '../../../components/Playbook.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: build the capability and the counterweight in the same decade, or you get the first alone. */}

I want to argue two things in one chapter, and they cut against each other.

The first is that our public administration still runs on the habits of the
typewriter era, that this wastes enormous amounts of human life, and that we
could fix it inside a decade. The second is that my own complaint is unfair,
because digitising a state is not a technical job. **A state becomes total as it
becomes digital.** The digital state and the total state are the same system
seen from two sides: the more of your life runs through it, the more completely
somebody at a console can reach into it.

Both halves are true at once. Anyone who only says the first is selling
software. Anyone who only says the second ends up defending the fax machine. The
question is what has to be built so that the first can happen without the
second eating us.

## The opportunity we are sitting on

Go into a public office and watch what happens to a piece of paper. Somebody
retypes what somebody else already typed. A form is checked against a register
the clerk cannot query directly. A case moves at the speed of an envelope. None
of this is anyone's fault; it is a set of procedures designed before the
machines existed that would make them unnecessary, and never redesigned after.

The potential in digitalisation and automation is enormous, and it is not mainly
about saving money. It is about quality of life: work nobody has to do by hand
any more, decisions that arrive in days instead of seasons, a citizen who can
see the state of their own case. The courts get something extra out of being
rebuilt properly — a system that records what it did, in order, as a by-product
of working at all. **Transparency you get for free because the thing was built
well is worth more than transparency somebody has to promise.**

In Poland there is a clock on this. The people who staff that administration
are leaving. My mother retires in two years, and that is roughly the window we
have to reform public administration before the knowledge that keeps it running
walks out of the building with the people who hold it. Nobody is queuing to
replace them at those wages, and most of that work does not need a human being
at all. I would not take one of those jobs, and I do not know many people who
would. That is the honest measure of how long this can be postponed.

## The objection I have to make against myself

Then somebody asks the question I cannot answer with code: **who rules the data,
and on what terms?**

<Callout kind="claim" label="Three properties of a digital state">
  Once the register is the truth, whoever controls the register controls what is
  true about you. Once identity is a credential rather than a face, the
  credential can be suspended. Once money is an entry in a ledger, the entry can
  be frozen, expired, or made conditional on behaviour. None of this needs
  anyone to have evil intentions; they are properties of the system, available
  to whoever holds it next.
</Callout>

This is why people protest against digital ID and digital currency, and the
protests are more rational than their opponents admit. The objection is not
technophobia. The objection is that **a switch exists, and somebody can turn a
person off.** You do not have to believe today's government would do it. You
have to notice that today's government is not the last one.

So my complaint about the typewriter-era state was unfair — not wrong, unfair.
Digitalisation was never a project for engineers to deliver and politics to
approve afterwards. The question of who governs the data is the harder half,
and it has to be settled first, in public, by the people whose lives run through
the thing.

## Why a digital state is a total state

"Total" here does not mean totalitarian. It means total in reach: a state that
touches everything, sees everything, and can act everywhere at once.

The old state was limited by friction. Surveillance cost people. Enforcement
cost time. If a government wanted to make your life impossible, somebody had to
do the work, and the work was expensive enough to be reserved for people who
mattered. Those costs are what protected ordinary citizens — not laws, friction.

A digital state removes the friction. That is the whole point of it and why it
delivers real benefits: the same property that lets a service reach you in a
second without an office visit lets a decision about you take effect in a second
without a hearing. You cannot keep one and refuse the other. They are the same
capability seen from two ends.

**The conclusion is not to stop building.** A state that refuses to digitalise
does not stay free; it stays slow, and eventually buys the systems anyway, late,
from someone else, on someone else's terms. The conclusion is that the power has
to be balanced at the same time as the capability is built.

## The counterweight

The balance I want is direct democracy, at every level where a decision is
made: the school, the municipality, the region, the nation, the Union.

Not as a mood, and not as consultation. As the two instruments with teeth that
[Direct Democracy](/book/direct-democracy#the-words-in-one-place) sets out: a
citizens' initiative to force a vote on a change, and an optional referendum to
strike down a law parliament has passed. Parliaments carry on — the precise name
is semi-direct democracy — and citizens decide specific questions, often, and
the result binds.

Then the relationship inverts. A state with total reach and citizens who can
overrule it between elections is a tool. A state with total reach and citizens
who can only complain for four years is something else, and we should say the
word out loud rather than discover it later.

<Callout kind="demand" label="The demand">
  Digital identity arrives together with universal direct democracy across the
  Union. Same package, same decade. Not the capability first and the
  accountability "in a later phase", because later phases are where
  accountability goes to die.
</Callout>

And the mirror of it, which is the uncomfortable part: **while no counterweight
ships alongside these systems, citizens are entitled to resist them.** Not
because resisting is wise — refusing digitalisation forever is a losing position
— but because the resistance is a correct reading of the deal on offer.
Governments across Europe have spent two decades failing at the ordinary things,
crisis after crisis, and are now asking for more direct power over people's
lives. Declining that trade is not superstition. It is arithmetic.

I would rather the demand were the other one: give us the vote and we will help
you build the system.

## Keep the paper

There is a cheap way to take most of the fear out of this, and I do not know why
it is not the default position.

<Playbook title="The order of build" steps={[
  { action: "Keep paper as the emergency layer of the state.", why: "Not only for voting — for the basic functions. Today's procedures stay in place, simplified if you like, as the fallback that works when the systems are down, when somebody has been switched off by mistake, or when a government has to be shown the old route still exists." },
  { action: "Vote in the school and the town hall first.", why: "We already vote in one room in a school; a town hall can do the same. If the cost of frequent votes is the objection, the honest response is to work out how to run them cheaply, in public — not to postpone." },
  { action: "Build the digital layer in parallel, as learning.", why: "Start now, make mistakes where they are survivable, and let it carry something serious only once it has proved in the open that it deserves to." },
  { action: "Build it as Europeans, together.", why: "One set of systems for identity, records and voting, designed jointly, with each country deploying and running its own. The engineering is done once; the sovereignty stays where it is; nobody depends on a platform they cannot inspect." },
]} />

A state that cannot operate without its database has handed whoever holds the
database a power nobody voted to give them.

<EvidenceBox title="What would show this can work">
  Nobody has done this at Union scale, so the chapter does not claim it works.
  Three pieces of work would settle it: whether a binding citizen vote can be
  given legal force at national and European level without rewriting the
  treaties; whether a jointly built identity system can be deployed nationally
  without creating one central operator with a switch; and whether frequent
  voting at municipal and regional level changes outcomes, which the Swiss
  record can answer better than speculation.
</EvidenceBox>

## What Central Europe puts in

This is where my part of Europe stops being a recipient and starts being a
contributor, and I would like that said plainly for once.

Poland and Central Europe have the software engineers. If the new Union needs a
digital administration, an autonomous health service, digital courts and
offices, a voting system nobody can quietly rig, then that is work we can
actually do, and it is what we should put into the common system rather than
another round of asking what we get out of it.

Germany built SAP: software that runs companies, sold to the world. **Europe
could build the system that runs a state** — digital administration, digital
democracy, predictive healthcare, digital courts — built here, deployed here
first, then exported, because every other democracy on earth will face the same
problem and most would rather not buy the answer from a superpower. That is the
difference between plumbing and an industry. We should aim at the industry.

<SideNote label="The system itself">
  What the shared core and the national deployments would contain, in detail:
  [European eGovernment](/book/european-egovernment).
</SideNote>

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "Want the digital state. The waste in the current one costs people years of their lives, and the staff who keep it standing are leaving within the decade.",
  "Demand the counterweight in the same breath. When somebody proposes digital identity, digital money or a national register, the question is not whether it is convenient. It is: what can I overrule, and how often? If the answer is nothing, every four years, the correct response is no.",
]}>
  Two things are worth holding at the same time, and most public argument makes
  you pick one.
</MeansForYou>
