# European eGovernment

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/european-egovernment


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: build the core once, deploy it nationally, and the governance question decides whether it is worth building. */}

This chapter is the shape of a system, not the argument for it. The argument
is in [The Total State](/book/the-total-state#why-a-digital-state-is-a-total-state):
a state becomes total as it becomes digital, so the capability and the
counterweight have to be built in the same decade. What follows is a proposal,
assembled from the author's dictation on how he would build the thing, and it
has not been adopted as a programme.

A **digital state** and the **total state** are the same system seen from two
sides. Everything below is the first side. The second side, who can overrule
it and how often, is not a later phase; it is the condition on which the first
side is worth building at all.

<Callout kind="claim" label="The condition, from The Total State">
  The governance question is the harder half, and it has to be settled first,
  in public, by the people whose lives run through the thing. Digital identity
  arrives together with universal direct democracy across the Union: same
  package, same decade.
</Callout>

## One core, twenty-seven deployments

Build it as Europeans, together. One set of systems for identity, for records,
for voting, designed jointly, with each country deploying and running its own.
The engineering gets done once. The sovereignty stays where it is. And nobody
ends up dependent on a platform they cannot inspect.

The author's own picture of it, in
[Redesigning the State](/book/redesigning-the-state#a-shared-core-your-own-deployment),
is closer to how large software is already built than to how administrations
are: every country and region gets its own deployment and decides how to
customise it, while the core, where the members have an enormous amount in
common, is shared. European digital startups then get built on top of it, on
European digital infrastructure, which today does not exist for them to build
on.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="What is shared, what is national, what stays on paper"
  columns={[
    { label: "Built once, shared", kind: "proposed" },
    { label: "Deployed and run nationally", kind: "proposed" },
    { label: "Kept on paper as the emergency layer", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "Identity", cells: ["The credential, its standards, the signature", "Who issues it, on what documents, who can suspend it and under what law", "A document that proves who you are when the credential is switched off"] },
    { dimension: "Registers and records", cells: ["Data model, interfaces, the audit trail that records what the state did and in what order", "The registers themselves, on national soil, under national law", "The basic civil acts, so that a life is not undone by a lost row"] },
    { dimension: "Voting", cells: ["The counting and audit machinery, built in the open", "The roll, the questions, the thresholds and safeguards", "Paper ballots in a school hall or town hall, always available, never a fallback that has to be argued for"] },
    { dimension: "Case handling", cells: ["The workflow engine, the citizen's view of their own case", "Language, branding, the local administrative structure and its exceptions", "Simplified paper procedures for the basic functions of the state"] },
    { dimension: "Rules", cells: ["Open standards for anything that extends the core", "Legal and administrative arrangements, which may differ by region and by function", "The old route, kept so a government can be shown it still exists"] },
  ]}
  source="Assembled from the author's dictation (direct-democracy dump, answers-and-safeguards dump, redesigning-the-state dump); the row contents are proposed, not adopted"
/>

Two rules run through every row. The core has to be cheap to run and hard to
monopolise, or it will be captured by whoever supplies it; that is the design
goal argued in [Cheap Is Wealth](/book/cheap-is-wealth), and this proposal is
one of the things it applies to. And the digital layer is built in parallel, as
learning: it starts now, makes its mistakes where mistakes are survivable, and
carries something serious only once it has proved, in the open, that it
deserves to.

## Systems by function, not by border

The more interesting part of the author's picture is that digital systems would
be distributed where they are needed, rather than along administrative borders.
An old Italian hill village, a Portuguese one and a town in Albania may be best
served by the same city system; a Scandinavian port city needs another; mountain
tourist towns and industrial towns another again. Different systems, deployed
where they fit, built and shared in common. The same could go for legal and
administrative arrangements, which may differ between regions according to the
function a region performs. The catalogue of such systems is what this chapter
would grow into; the two paragraphs above are all that has been dictated.

## Paper is the emergency layer

Keep paper as the emergency layer of the state. Not only for voting: for the
basic functions generally. The procedures that run today on paper stay in
place, simplified if you like, as the fallback that works when the systems are
down, when somebody has been switched off by mistake, or when a government has
to be shown that the old route still exists. A state that cannot operate
without its database has handed whoever holds the database a power nobody voted
to give them. The argument for this is in
[The Total State](/book/the-total-state#keep-the-paper); here it is a row in
the table, on purpose.

## What Central Europe puts in

Poland and Central Europe have the software engineers; that is a labour-market
fact anyone in the industry recognises, and the author's own claim about what
his part of Europe contributes. If the Union needs a digital administration, an
autonomous health service, digital courts and offices and a voting system
nobody can quietly rig, that is work we can do, and it is what we should put
into the common system. Germany's complex administration, carried into the
digital world with its complexity intact, is the role the author would offer
Germany; that offer is labelled as his idea, not an agreed plan, in
[Redesigning the State](/book/redesigning-the-state#an-offer-to-germany).

<ObjectionList title="The objections that survived the merge">
  <Objection claim="Shared infrastructure means one central operator with a switch." verdict="Answered on paper; not yet answered in practice.">
    The design answer is that the core is code and standards, and every
    deployment is national: nobody outside the country runs the country's
    registers. Whether a jointly built identity system can in fact be deployed
    nationally without creating one central operator is one of the three things
    The Total State says would settle its own argument, and it is not settled.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Twenty-seven legacy systems will not migrate to one core." verdict="Probably right, and no timeline is offered.">
    The earlier drafts of this chapter promised phases and years. They are gone,
    because nothing behind them was more than a guess. What can be said is that
    a core deployed in parallel, as learning, does not require anyone to
    migrate on a date; it requires one function to work in two countries.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Digital divides: the people the state most needs to reach are the least online." verdict="This is what the paper layer is for.">
    A state that keeps its paper procedures as a permanent layer, not a
    transition, does not have a digital-divide problem in the sense the
    objection means. It has two routes, and the slow one still works.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

<EvidenceBox title="What would show the core can exist">

One function, a birth registration or a business registration, built once and
deployed in two member states with different administrative law, running for a
year, with the code and the audit trail public. If it works, the shared core is
real and the rest is scope. If it cannot be done for one function, the whole
proposal is a diagram.

</EvidenceBox>

Want the digital state; demand the counterweight in the same breath. That
sentence belongs to [The Total State](/book/the-total-state); this chapter
exists so that when somebody asks what the digital state would actually be,
there is one page that says so, and it says so on the total state's terms.

  source={[

# Robotic Reindustrialisation

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/robotic-reindustrialisation

import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import PullQuote from '../../../components/PullQuote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';
import { default as T } from '../../../components/TermRef.astro';

{/* SPINE: the war is already paying for the robots; make sure the civilian demand is waiting when the wartime customer goes, and keep the machines cheap. */}

This is the top of the stack, and it only works because of what sits
underneath it. [The demographic argument](/book/designing-our-retirement) says
why we need it: there will not be enough people to do the work our retirement
depends on. A [common working language](/vision#language) is what lets the
engineers who build it work with each other. A [digital
state](/book/the-total-state) is what it plugs into. Robotics on its own,
without those, is a trade fair.

What follows is how Europe could actually get there.

## Europe needs a new industry anyway

The old engine was the car. It is being taken apart — by electrification, by
Chinese manufacturing, by a shift in what a vehicle even is — and the Union's
own electric-car transition has been half reversed to keep the car companies
alive. Germany knows this better than anyone, and so does every supplier town
from Bavaria to Silesia that grew up around it.

Robotics is the natural successor. It needs precision manufacturing, which
Europe has; industrial engineering culture, which Europe has; and software,
which Europe has been losing at — and which is exactly where Central Europe can
contribute something the rest of the continent needs. Germany could rebuild its
entire car industry to produce robots, and be an industrial-robotic power. So
this is not only a demographic defence. It is the reindustrialisation Europe was
going to have to attempt regardless, aimed at a problem that makes it urgent.

## What Poland and Central Europe bring

Every member state asks what it can offer the Union that the Union actually
wants. For Poland the honest answer is software, and a share in building the
machines. The layer around robotics — control systems, fleet coordination,
simulation, safety, the integration work that decides whether a machine is
deployable or a demo — is software work at industrial scale. Poles are good at
software; the Germans built SAP. In robotics the software *is* the product;
the metal is a commodity.

That is worth stating plainly, because Central Europe has spent twenty years
as the place where other people's systems get maintained. This is a chance to
own a layer — and to export it, rather than only run it at home.

## The path runs through the war

Here is the uncomfortable part, and skipping it would make everything above
wishful. Europe is in a conflict with Russia, and that conflict is already
doing what peacetime industrial policy never managed: pushing serious money
into autonomy, sensing, drones, and the manufacturing capacity to build them at
volume. Defence budgets are funding robotics research right now, at a scale no
civilian programme was ever going to get approved.

<Callout kind="claim" label="The strategy">
  Stimulate the market now through defence, and convert the sector to civilian
  purposes after the war — the same autonomy, sensing and manufacturing
  capacity, pointed at demographic collapse instead of at an enemy.
</Callout>

**That capacity converts.** Autonomous navigation, machine perception,
teleoperation, ruggedised actuators, and above all the factories and supply
chains that produce them are the capabilities the civilian problem needs. A
drone company and an agricultural robotics company are separated by their
customers, not by their engineering. No committee needs to schedule the
conversion: when the wartime customer goes away, the capacity looks for a new
one, and demographic collapse will be the largest market in Europe. Industrial
policy's job is to know this in advance and make sure the civilian demand is
waiting — procurement, standards and pilot deployments ready on the other side.
What this is not: an argument for prolonging anything. It is an argument for
making sure the industrial base built under one pressure survives to answer the
next one, instead of collapsing with the contracts.

<EvidenceBox>
  Whether defence-funded autonomy actually converts is checkable: a count of
  European suppliers that entered military autonomy after 2022 and now carry a
  civilian product line, against those that did not. Nobody has published one.
  If the number is small, the conversion needs to be planned harder than this
  chapter assumes; if it is zero, the strategy is wrong.
</EvidenceBox>

## Where the machines go first

In the order they are ready, not in the order they are exciting.

**Municipal and communal services.** Cleaning, maintenance, waste,
groundskeeping, basic logistics — heavily staffed, highly mechanical, already
short of workers, and operating in spaces a city controls. The easiest place to
deploy and the fastest place to feel the benefit. I would not bet on humanoids
here. I would bet on simple machines: the ones that take the rubbish out, the
ones that cut the grass, the ones that drive.

**Food production and delivery.** Autonomous farming and autonomous transport
are the most advanced civilian robotics we have. Food security stops being
theoretical when the people who grow and move it are retiring.

<SideNote label="In the frame">
  The same three targets, in the same order, as the frame's table:
  [Designing Our Retirement](/book/designing-our-retirement#the-case-for-machines).
</SideNote>

<PullQuote>Being cared for by a machine and being alone are not the same thing.</PullQuote>

**Predictive medicine and healthcare.** The cost that grows fastest as a
population ages. Robotics here means less a machine at the bedside than an
entire system that catches what would have become a hospitalisation.

**And the part that is not machinery at all:** systems that let older people
support each other, live together, work if they want to, and stay in contact.
Being cared for by a machine and being alone are not the same thing. We are
designing the world we retire into, and it should be one worth arriving in.

## Cheap beats owned

The gains from this can be captured by a handful of firms, and by default they
will be. <T slug="who-captures-the-gains">Who captures the gains</T> is the
question every proposal on this site has to answer, and my answer is that
ownership is the second question: what matters first is that the machines are
<T slug="cheap-is-wealth">cheap</T> — affordable, easy to implement, built on
open standards, hard to monopolise. A machine a municipality can buy from four
suppliers, repair locally and run on software that is not a rental does not
need a complicated ownership theory. A locked platform with a per-hour licence
concentrates its returns no matter who signs the contract.

<SideNote label="Argued in full">
  Why cheapness, not ownership, is the design goal: [Cheap Is
  Wealth](/book/cheap-is-wealth). Who the surplus must reach: [Who It Earns
  For](/book/who-it-earns-for).
</SideNote>

<ObjectionList title="The objection I raised myself">
  <Objection claim="The robots run on chips and rare metals Europe does not have." verdict="Probably the weakest link, and not yet written.">
    True. The machines depend on microprocessors made from rare metals sourced
    across the whole world, on AI centres, and on enough political stability
    and purchasing power to keep buying them. For the robots to exist, a whole
    mass of things has to be organised — this is one of them, and the site does
    not yet have a chapter on it.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

## What has to happen

- **Treat robotics as national and European strategy**, the way energy and
  defence are treated — not as a research topic.
- **Plan the conversion before it is needed**: civilian procurement, standards
  and pilot programmes waiting for the capacity built under defence contracts.
- **Cheap, open and hard to monopolise** as the condition every deployment has
  to meet, decided as policy because the market will not decide it in our
  favour.
- **Deploy in municipal services first**, where the public sector is both
  customer and beneficiary, and where results are visible to citizens within a
  budget cycle.
- **Let Central Europe own the software layer**, deliberately, as industrial
  strategy rather than subcontracting.

<MeansForYou actions={["If you build control systems, perception, fleet software or mechanical design: this is the largest problem available in Europe, and it has a deadline, a customer and a funding source that already exists.", "Start with a piece that runs. The Union will not commission this from the top; the pieces turn out to work, and the policy catches up to what is already running."]}>
  A demonstration is worth more than a strategy paper.
</MeansForYou>

<ProvenanceNote
  source={[
    "aging-society-frame.md:83-109 (the ceiling; the path through the war), :140-148 (robotics arriving anyway; a new automotive industry; Poland and Polish software), :153-162 (ownership second, cheap first), :195-197 (what Poland can offer)",
    "2026-09-25-direct-democracy-dump.md:91-96 (chips, rare metals, stability), :229-238 (Poles and software, SAP, an export product), :299-305 (Germany rebuilds its car industry for robots; simple robots before humanoids)",

  ]}

    "A new automotive industry as Europe's opening; Germany could rebuild its car industry to produce robots; simple robots (rubbish, groundskeeping, driving) before humanoids.",
    "Poland's and Central Europe's contribution is software; Poles are good at software, Germany built SAP; export it.",

  ]}

  ]}
  cut={[

    "The fourth full statement of the ownership argument — one home.",
    "The bullet summary that restated the chapter — kept the bullets as the asks, cut the restatement.",
  ]}
  open={["None."]}

# European Science

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/european-science


import KeyFigure from '../../../components/KeyFigure.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: no shared language, no shared science, no European AI; and psychology is where the method can be proved fastest. */}

Ask why Europe has no AI of its own and you will get answers about venture
capital, energy prices and regulation. I think the answer is older and duller
than that.

Perhaps there is no European AI because there is no European science, and there
is no European science because we do not speak English together.

## What we have and what we do not

We do have joint research. There is CERN. But look at what it is: theoretical
physics, one place, one narrow field, somewhere people go on trips. Now look at
the fields that will decide the next twenty years, the practical ones that
actually count: artificial intelligence, robotics, bioengineering. There is no
place where researchers from every member state sit next to each other, day
after day, shoulder to shoulder, and work on those.

{/* ASK-1 (answers-and-safeguards-dump.md:105): the transcript reads "Jest orgazmus [CERN?]"; CERN is the transcriber's guess, consistent with "fizyka teoretyczna". Confirm CERN is what you meant. */}

| What Europe has | What Europe does not have |
|---|---|
| Conferences | A room |
| Consortia that file reports | People from every country working side by side on one hard problem |
| A shared physics laboratory | A shared laboratory for AI, robotics or bioengineering |
| Twenty-four official languages | One working language for science |

Sitting in one room requires being able to talk in it. That is not a detail you
can solve later with better funding; it is the floor everything else stands on,
which is why [European English](/book/european-english) comes first in this
book and this chapter comes after it. Language integration is upstream of
European science, and European science is upstream of European business. If we
get the first one, the most able people in Europe can work together. If we do
not, they will keep working for someone else, in English, somewhere else.

## What a European science would work on

Not everything. Our problems.

Europe is old and getting older; that is the whole argument of
[Designing Our Retirement](/book/designing-our-retirement), and it points at a
short list of things worth putting money and talent into: predictive medicine,
longevity and healthy life, psychology, artificial intelligence,
bioengineering.

Predictive medicine is the one people understand least. The nearest definition
in the literature is what Leroy Hood called P4 medicine, predictive, preventive,
personalised and participatory
([Hood and Flores, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nbt.2012.03.004)): instead
of waiting for disease to declare itself and then treating it, you use data to
estimate who is heading toward it and act early. Treating diabetes is medicine.
Knowing five years out that this person is heading for diabetes, and changing
the course, is predictive medicine. For a continent with a shrinking
working-age population, the difference between those two is the difference
between a health service we can afford and one we cannot.

But the interesting work is not only the medical science. It is everything
around it, and almost none of it is done:

- How do you program the AI that does this, and how do you build a health
  service around it rather than bolting it onto the side?
- How do you measure all of it, so that the system learns from the medical
  data?
- How do you make that safe, and how do you learn from the data at all?
- How do you keep improving the whole system once it is running?
- And the question underneath all of them: are our research methods actually
  good, and are we studying the right things?

That last one is not a rhetorical flourish. A research programme that never
checks whether its own methods work will produce a large amount of confident
nothing.

Above all, European scientists should be the ones sitting over European medical
data. This should be a European project, since we already have the rules on
personal data. The **European Health Data Space**, Regulation (EU) 2025/327, in
force since 26 March 2025, is the legal route for reusing health data across
borders for research and policy, through data access bodies, permits and secure
processing environments, on top of GDPR
([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2025/327/oj)). The rules exist.
The science that should be using them does not exist in the same way. We built
the door and no one built the building behind it.

## European universities

If the point is people from every country working shoulder to shoulder, it has
to be built as such. European universities, taking people from across the
Union, with no dominance of any one nation: not a French institute with foreign
guests, not a German one; ours.

Where they go, I do not know. In all the cities that want the AI centres, or
somewhere next to them. Or perhaps they should not be there at all. What does
not depend on the map: people from different countries have to work on
artificial intelligence here, and the same goes for bioengineering, and the
same goes for psychology.

## Mental health is an illness, not a personal failing

That last one is where I would start, because it is the largest untreated
problem we have and the one where the method can be tested fastest.

I think what we are looking at is a civilisational illness, and it comes from
having changed the way we live very fast. We did not get enough social support,
and we did not see how relationships work between different people: not only
our parents and children in a closed home, where we are hostages of our
parents, with no aunt, no uncle, no grandmother to go to, cry at, hug, ask for
something, and use to balance the power of the parents. Only those parents, who
are themselves stressed by work and by carrying the whole responsibility for the
family, in a way that was not true before. On top of that, parents keep
children at home, under a bell jar, so they do not get enough social skill or
social awareness.

You cannot learn to read other people without other people to read.

The conclusion I draw is not that anyone failed. It is that this should be
treated the way we treat illness, which it probably is: something that gets
diagnosed, treated and supported, without shame. Not a private weakness you are
supposed to fix on your own time.

## Therapy at scale

Who, if not the state, is to stand behind the chatbots?

Millions of people already confide in them. OpenAI, I am told, hires
psychologists. But somebody has to stand behind the chatbots that people bring
their problems to, and start helping them put those problems in order, in an
organised way. This could not be done with therapy alone; it can be done with
intelligent chatbots. From inside the conversation the system should be able to
say: this is the kind of thing a therapist deals with, would you like to hand
this over and talk to a human therapist? Behind the chatbot there is a human
therapist, funded by the state, helping the chatbot, or even a panel of them.
They can switch you over digitally, if you agree. I think many people will
agree, if the care on the other side is good.

<KeyFigure
  qualifier="≈"
  value="70 / 30"
  label="of therapeutic work that could be automated or half-automated, against the share that should stay human; the author's rough split, not a measurement"
  source="Dictated 2026-09-25 (redesigning-the-state dump, lines 244–252); nobody has measured it"
  aside
/>

With AI we can research, measure and test an enormous amount: psychological
things, therapeutic things. What a therapist once had to do with a person, we
can automate or half-automate. My rough estimate, and I want it read as an
estimate and not a finding, is that around seventy per cent of therapeutic work
can be automated and around thirty per cent should stay with a human. Nobody
has measured this. Measuring it is exactly the kind of thing a European science
of psychology should do.

The thirty matters more than the seventy. It is a human who has contact with
the patient, meets them from time to time and talks, and, this is the part
people miss, shares their own feelings and insight with the agent; that gives
the agent a human perspective. That person is also the supervisor of the
therapy. Perhaps several people are: one therapist who holds the meetings, and
two supervisors who follow the case and talk it over weekly or monthly. Care at
scale, with humans where humans are irreplaceable, and oversight that is plural
rather than a single overworked person.

<ObjectionList title="The two objections, answered as I would answer them">
  <Objection claim="There are nowhere near enough therapists, and there never will be." verdict="Correct, and it is the reason for the design, not against it.">
    On the old model the supply of care is capped by how many trained humans
    can sit in a room for an hour. That is how the shortfall gets closed: not by
    training ten times more therapists, which will not happen, but by putting
    the scarce human hours where they count and letting the machine carry the
    rest, under supervision.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="People will not hand their worst moments to a state-backed system. It is a privacy question." verdict="Less than it looks.">
    Many people have similar problems. If it is treated as an illness, which it
    probably is, one that is treated and supported, then the handover is
    consent to care, not surveillance. It happens only if the person agrees, and
    I think many will, if the care is good.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

The same logic runs outward from there. Psychologists at the back of every
large event, and visible information about the other ways of coping: therapy,
therapists from the different schools, the reasonably sensible ones, people who
can spot a problem, help from another angle, say that perhaps this would suit
you better than that. And the personal-development and psychology market
regulated, because at the moment anyone can sell anything to people at their
worst.

<EvidenceBox title="The first study a European psychology should run">

Whether the split above is anywhere near right: take one condition with a
standard therapeutic protocol, run it with a supervised agent doing the
structured work and a human doing the rest, and publish the outcomes against
the fully human arm. That one study would also test the method this chapter is
about: whether European scientists over European data, under the rules we
already wrote, can answer a European question faster than anyone else.

</EvidenceBox>

None of this works without the research underneath it. Which is the point of
the chapter: a European science, on European problems, with European scientists
over European data, and mental health as the first thing large enough, and
neglected enough, to prove whether we can do it.

<ProvenanceNote
  source={[
    "2026-09-25-answers-and-safeguards-dump.md:102-113 (why there is no European AI)",
    "2026-09-25-redesigning-the-state-dump.md:184-252 (psychology, chatbots, civilisational illness, European science, the 70/30 split)",
  ]}
  dictated={[
    "Perhaps there is no European AI because there is no European science and we do not speak English; something exists, but theoretical physics, trips, not people from every country side by side on AI and robotics; language integration comes first (:104-113)",
    "European science on European problems: predictive medicine, psychology, longevity; how to program the AI, build the health service, measure and learn safely, verify our own methods; European scientists over European data, since we have the data rules (:228-235)",
    "European universities with people from all of Europe, no national dominance; where they go he does not know (:237-242)",
    "A civilisational illness from a changed way of living; no aunt or grandmother to balance the parents; children under a bell jar (:205-212)",
    "The state behind the chatbots; a human therapist funded by the state behind the bot, or a panel; digital handover with consent; not a privacy question; treated as an illness (:192-203)",
    "About 70 % automatable, 30 % human; the human shares insight with the agent and supervises; one therapist and two supervisors (:244-252)",
    "Psychologists at large events; information about other routes; regulate the personal-development market (:186-190)",
  ]}
  added={[
    "P4 medicine as the nearest definition of predictive medicine, with a source: offered",
    "The European Health Data Space as Regulation (EU) 2025/327, in force 26 March 2025: sourced, checked 2026-09-25",
    "The have/lack table, the objection list and the evidence box: editorial structure of his claims",
    "'OpenAI, I am told, hires psychologists': his 'podobno', kept as hearsay, unsourced",
  ]}
  cut={[
    "His personal account of emotional isolation (:214-224): unpublished by default (R4 Q7) until he says otherwise",
    "The manifesto's copy of the 'no European AI' argument belongs here, not there (one argument, one home); nothing cut from this chapter on that account",
    "One of two hedges before the mental-health conclusion",
  ]}
  open={["ASK-1"]}
/>

# The Shorter Week

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/the-shorter-week


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import { default as T } from '../../../components/TermRef.astro';

{/* SPINE: the freed hours are the only place the time for learning and for deciding things can come from, and four days must be the legal anchor or it becomes a pay cut. */}

The [manifesto](/manifesto#the-work-is-going-away-and-that-is-the-time-we-need)
says the work is going away and that this is the time we need. This chapter is
the practical form of that sentence. If the time is real, somebody has to say
where it comes from, who pays for it and what it is for. Otherwise it arrives
as unemployment, which is the same hours with none of the money and none of the
dignity.

There are two ways a society can receive a jump in productivity. It can take it
as fewer people working, with the rest thrown out and told they failed. Or it
can take it as everyone working less. The second is a choice, not a mechanism.
Nothing about a machine decides which one you get.

## Lifelong learning is a slogan until you free the days

Every serious document about the next twenty years says the same thing: people
will have to keep learning, skills will go stale faster than careers, and we
are genuinely asking whether we can keep up with AI at all. Then the same
document leaves the working week at five days and says nothing more.

You cannot learn a new trade in the evening after a full week, with children in
the house. Almost nobody does. Lifelong learning is not a question of will or
of platforms or of another funded programme of certificates. It is a question
of days. If we mean it, we have to take the days out of the week and give them
to people.

<Callout kind="demand" label="The demand">
  Two days a week for something else. Study, if you want to study. Your own
  projects, if you are building something. Your children. Rest. It is not the
  state's business which. The state's business is that the days exist.
</Callout>

## Where to cut, and why there

Not everywhere at once, and not by decree in the abstract. Cut the week where
the machines demonstrably took the work.

Start with services, where AI already took a great deal of it — support, back
office, translation, routine analysis. The output is being produced with fewer
hours. Shorten the week there by a day and the same work still gets done,
because it is already getting done that way.

Then the factories, as the robots arrive. [Robotic
Reindustrialisation](/book/robotic-reindustrialisation) argues that Europe has
to build those lines anyway, because we will not have the workers. When a line
is automated, the hours it used to need do not disappear from the economy; they
disappear from somebody's life. Shorten the week on that line.

The end state I have in mind is four days for most people and three for some.
Not one uniform week. A range, with four as the default.

## Pay: make four days the normal week in law

The objection is immediate and fair: a four-day week where the fifth day is
simply unpaid is a pay cut of a fifth with a friendly name. That is how this
reform fails.

The answer is to move the legal anchor. **Redefine the minimum wage as pay for
four days, not five.** The fifth day is paid on top. A person working five days
earns more than a person working four, but the floor — the number the law
protects, the number a full-time job is measured against — covers four.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="What changes in the pay rules"
  columns={[
    { label: "Today" },
    { label: "Under this proposal", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "The minimum wage covers", cells: ["Five days", "Four days"] },
    { dimension: "The fifth day", cells: ["Part of the floor", "Paid on top of it"] },
    { dimension: "Weekend work", cells: ["Varies by sector and contract", "Priced higher — ten per cent more, in the author's rough figure"] },
    { dimension: "Sunday", cells: ["Varies by sector and contract", "Higher still"] },
    { dimension: "The default week", cells: ["Five days", "Four; three for some; five or six by choice, paid properly"] },
  ]}
  source="The right-hand column is the author's proposal; the weekend figure is his estimate from the 2026-09-25 dictation, not a costed rate"
/>

That is the whole mechanism: a set of incentives arranged so that the cheapest,
most ordinary thing an employer can do is offer four days. Today the incentives
point the other way, and that is the only reason five days feels natural.

## Flexibility that runs both ways

A shorter week must not become a new uniform. Some people want more hours, not
fewer.

Take my own case. I have not worked for seven months. I spend my days building
things with AI — including this site. In the system I am describing I could go
and work Friday, Saturday and Sunday at weekend rates, three long days, and
keep four for what I am actually doing. I would earn a living and keep the
project. Right now the labour market offers me either a full week or nothing,
so I take nothing and live off savings. That is not flexibility; that is a
market with one setting.

And there are people on the other side of it — building a business, saving for
something, simply wanting the money — who should be able to take five days or
six and be paid properly for them. The point is not to force anyone into
leisure. The point is that the default should be four, and that the deviations
in both directions should be priced honestly.

## Why this is not about leisure

This site argues for [direct democracy](/book/direct-democracy): that citizens
should hold an initiative and a veto over the laws that govern them, and decide
the direction of the Union rather than ratify it every four years. The
strongest objection to that argument is that people do not have time to think.
They are tired, they are working, they will vote on a headline.

That objection is correct under a five-day week. It is a statement about
schedules, not about people's intelligence.

A citizenry that decides things needs time to read, argue and change its mind.
Nobody is going to hand that time over out of civic good will. It has to come
from somewhere, and the only place it can come from is the working week — which
is precisely where automation is about to create a surplus. The freed hours and
the democratic deficit are the same problem seen from two sides. The same goes
for the rest of what this book asks for: rebuilding the state, [paying for our
own retirement](/book/designing-our-retirement), learning fast enough to stay
useful next to the machines. All of it needs a population with hours to spare.
We are about to have the hours. The question is whether anyone arranges them
into anything — and whether the gains that free them reach the people whose
hours they were, which is the question of <T slug="who-captures-the-gains">who
captures the gains</T>, argued in [Cheap Is Wealth](/book/cheap-is-wealth).

{/* ASK-1 (education-migration-workweek-dump.md:95-99): the link from the freed hours to the time direct democracy needs joins two of your dictations (lifelong learning here; referendums every three months in the direct-democracy dump). It is written without first person. Adopt it as yours? */}

<ObjectionList title="The holes, in order of size" intro="Three objections the proposal has not closed. The first is the real one.">
  <Objection claim="A nurse's output is hours." verdict="The genuine hole in the argument.">
    A nurse, a bus driver, a carer, a teacher in a classroom: their output is
    not going to be automated in the next decade, and a four-day week there
    means hiring more of them, in professions already short-staffed. Two honest
    answers exist — pay much more and treat the extra staff as a public
    investment, or accept that the shorter week arrives later in those sectors
    than in the automated ones — and the chapter does not choose between them.
    Anyone saying it is costless there is not being straight with you.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Who pays for the fifth day?" verdict="The cut follows the automation, sector by sector.">
    If the productivity gain is real, the gain pays for it — plausible in an
    automated service company, not in a firm where the machines have not
    arrived. Cutting the week there means raising prices or cutting profit, and
    somebody has to say which. That is why the demand reads "where the machines
    demonstrably took the work" and not "everywhere by 2030". What counts as
    demonstrably, and who measures it, is open.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="A floor can be eroded." verdict="Needs closing, by someone who knows the law.">
    The minimum-wage redefinition moves the floor rather than relying on good
    employers, which is the right shape. But a floor can be got around by hiring
    people as contractors, splitting jobs, pushing work off the books. Anyone
    who has watched labour law knows those moves. They would need closing, and
    how is not in this chapter.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

## What has actually been tried

The evidence exists and the research behind this chapter found it; here is
what it shows and what it does not.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="The two trials the headlines cite, beside the proposal"
  columns={[
    { label: "Iceland 2015–19", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "United Kingdom 2022", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "This proposal", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "Who", cells: ["Public sector, about 2,500 workers", "61 firms, about 2,900 workers, all volunteers", "Every sector where machines took the work"] },
    { dimension: "The week", cells: ["35–36 hours", "Four days", "Four days; three for some"] },
    { dimension: "Pay", cells: ["Unchanged", "Unchanged", "Minimum wage redefined as four days"] },
    { dimension: "How it was set", cells: ["Agreement", "Choice", "Law"] },
    { dimension: "What it showed", cells: ["Output held; wellbeing rose", "Revenue steady; resignations and burnout fell; most kept it", "Untested"] },
  ]}
  source="Autonomy and Alda (Iceland); Autonomy, Boston College and Cambridge (UK pilot) — links below"
/>

The honest caveat, which the headlines dropped: Iceland's trials cut the week
to roughly 35–36 hours, not to four days, and [researchers writing in The
Conversation](https://theconversation.com/the-success-of-icelands-four-day-week-trial-has-been-greatly-overstated-164083)
argued the result was widely overstated for exactly that reason. The [Autonomy
and Alda report](https://autonomy.work/portfolio/icelandsww/) is evidence that a
shorter week can be done without losing output. It is not evidence for four
days.

The UK pilot is closer. [The
results](https://autonomy.work/portfolio/uk4dwpilotresults/) report revenue
broadly steady, sharp falls in resignations and absence, and large drops in
reported burnout; a [follow-up a year
later](https://autonomy.work/portfolio/making-it-stick/) found most
participating organisations had kept the policy and about half had made it
permanent. What that is: strong evidence that firms which volunteered for a
four-day week mostly kept it and did not fall apart. What it is not: evidence
about firms that did not volunteer, about hospitals and buses, or about what
happens when the week is shortened by law rather than by choice. I am arguing
for something larger than has been tested, and I would rather say so.

<EvidenceBox>
  Not an essay. Pick a sector where AI has measurably taken hours, cut the week
  there with the four-day minimum wage attached, and publish output, wages,
  staffing and sick leave before and after. Then do the same in a hospital and
  publish the bill.
</EvidenceBox>

I am not a politician and I do not have the legislative text. I am someone who
thinks the freed time is the largest thing about to happen to Europe, and that
we are on course to waste it as unemployment, resentment and eventually war —
which is what the [manifesto](/manifesto) says, and the reason I am writing any
of this down.

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "If you run a team where AI took the hours, try four days at the same pay and publish the numbers. The trials that exist were all volunteers; be one that reports.",
  "If you know how to close the holes named above — the hospital, the contractor loophole — send the fix. I would rather hear it than be right.",
]}>
  Four days, three for some, the minimum wage measured over four, the weekend
  priced properly. That is the proposal.
</MeansForYou>

<ProvenanceNote
  source="2026-09-25-education-migration-workweek-dump.md:88-120 (the week), :95-99 (lifelong learning), :136-142 (activist, not politician)"
  dictated={[
    "Four and three days; two days a week for something else, for instance study (:90-93)",
    "Lifelong learning is how we keep up with AI, and it is implemented by shortening the week (:95-99)",
    "Cut in services where AI took the work, by a day, mandatory; then the factories as robots arrive; employers compensate (:100-106)",
    "The minimum wage is pay for four days, five is extra; a system of incentives with four as the default; own projects, travel, rest, children (:106-110)",
    "Some prefer three weekend days and four for themselves; his own case — months without work, building with AI; weekend rates ten per cent more, Sunday more (:112-120)",
    "Not a politician, an activist; asks for help (:136-142)",
  ]}
  added={[
    "The link between the freed hours and the time direct democracy needs — proposed (ASK-1)",
    "The three holes, and the Iceland and UK trials with sources — proposed",

  ]}
  open={["ASK-1"]}
/>

# New Cities

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/new-cities


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import KeyFigure from '../../../components/KeyFigure.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';
import SourceList from '../../../components/SourceList.astro';
import { default as T } from '../../../components/TermRef.astro';

{/* SPINE: a new standard of what a person must be given is due, and towers and large flats are what taking it seriously looks like. */}

Capital will not build you a large flat. It has no reason to. Rent is the point
of the exercise, and rent is highest where space is scarce, so scarcity is the
product. That is the housing form of the question this site asks of every
proposal — <T slug="who-captures-the-gains">who captures the gains</T> — and
this chapter is about the one actor that can decide otherwise, and what I think
it should decide.

It is an anti-capitalist idea and I will not pretend it is anything else:
capital drains rent out of us, year after year, for the ground we stand on. The
state can take a field in the middle of nowhere — buy it, or use land it already
holds — and say: here, on this nothing, we are building a town under new rules.
Or it sells the land for development on the condition that the new rules apply.
Either way the rules come first and the ground is cheap, which is the only
moment when any of this is affordable. Whether that makes the programme
communist is argued once, in [Who It Earns
For](/book/who-it-earns-for#is-this-communism), not here.

## Build beside the cities that exist

The empty field is the clean case. The useful case is next to a city that is
already there: take the land at its edge and build a district of towers, or of
ten-storey blocks.

<Callout kind="demand" label="The rule">
  Set a minimum height rather than a maximum — below this many floors you may
  not build here at all — and lay the tram or the metro with the sewers, before
  the first resident moves in.
</Callout>

That inversion is the whole policy in one line. Every planning system I have
lived under caps how high you may build; cap it the other way. And the rail is
not promised for the second phase, not "subject to future funding", because a
district that opens without rail is a district of cars forever, and you will
not retrofit it later at any price you are willing to pay.

## Space is the value

I want large flats. Eighty square metres, a hundred, a hundred and twenty. A
hundred and sixty. Two hundred.

That sounds extravagant until you ask what it is for. A family needs rooms. A
person who works from home needs a room that is not the kitchen table. And part
of a flat does not need to be heated to twenty-one degrees all winter: a
workshop space, heated lightly or not at all, plus a terrace. Once you stop
insisting that every square metre be a heated living room, square metres get
much cheaper — and [cheap is the goal](/book/cheap-is-wealth), not a side
effect — and you can hand people the thing they actually lack, which is room.

We are animals that did not grow up in a cave. We spent almost all of our
history outside and almost none of it there now, and I suspect that is why our
eyes are going: we look at close things all day. So when I ask for terraces,
distance to look at and something green at the bottom of the building, I am not
asking for decoration.

<SideNote label="What the research found">
  The suspicion has support: a three-year randomised trial in Guangzhou found
  that forty minutes of outdoor time at school cut the incidence of myopia in
  first-graders from 39.5% to 30.4%
  ([JAMA, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.10803)), and
  the [Cochrane review](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD013549.pub2/abstract)
  treats time outdoors as a modest, uncertain preventive measure. Offered, not
  load-bearing.
</SideNote>

{/* ASK-1 (redesigning-the-state-dump.md:157-158): you said "podobno" about the eyes. The trial is real; do you want it carrying weight in a housing chapter, or should it go? */}

And the way to have space without eating the countryside is to build high.
Density and space are not opposites; tall buildings are how you get both. We
have no third continent of land to spread onto.

<KeyFigure value="16.9%" label="of people in the EU lived in an overcrowded household in 2024; Romania 40.7%, Latvia 39.3%, Poland 33.7%" source="Eurostat, 2025" href="https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20251222-1" />

## A standard is due

Here is the spine of the argument, and it is not about towers.

After the industrial revolution we worked out what a person must be given so
that the institutions we depend on — family, school, medicine — could function
at all, and wrote it into building law. The research behind this chapter puts a
date on that: Britain's [Public Health Act of
1875](https://www.cieh.org/about-us/history-of-cieh/150-years-of-public-health-act/)
obliged local authorities to set byelaws, and new housing had to have drainage,
ventilation, a toilet, minimum space between buildings. Those were not luxuries.
They were the conditions under which the institutions could work, written into
law because exhortation had failed for fifty years.

That standard is now out of date. It says nothing about prevention, about
whether a body gets moved during the day, about daylight or distance or room to
work at home, or whether a child can get outside without being driven. We know
much more about what breaks people than we did in 1875 and have written almost
none of it into the rules for how we build.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="What the old standard required, and what a new one would add"
  columns={[
    { label: "1875", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "The standard due now", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "Water and waste", cells: ["Drainage and a toilet", "Unchanged"] },
    { dimension: "Air and light", cells: ["Ventilation", "Daylight, and distance to look at"] },
    { dimension: "Space", cells: ["A minimum gap between buildings", "Large flats; an unheated workshop part; a terrace"] },
    { dimension: "Movement", cells: ["—", "A gym in every building, open late, with a window on distance"] },
    { dimension: "Transport", cells: ["—", "Rail laid before occupancy"] },
    { dimension: "Ground", cells: ["—", "Something green at the foot of the block; allotments at the edge"] },
  ]}
  source="Public Health Act 1875 (CIEH); the right-hand column is the author's proposal"
/>

So write a new one. Movement, space, daylight, transport and green ground
designed in at the start rather than retrofitted by a later generation that
cannot afford it. The towers and the large flats are what it looks like when
you take that seriously.

Two items in the right-hand column are Polish, or nearly. Allotment gardens —
*ogrody działkowe*, [tens of thousands of
hectares](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/10/11/3829) of them in and around the
cities, plot by plot — give a person in a flat a piece of ground, a shed, a few
fruit trees. I recommend them without reservation; if other countries want one
Polish institution, take this one. And a gym in every building: not a fitness
industry, not a membership, a room in the block, open late or around the clock,
with weights and a bike and a window that looks out at distance. It costs almost
nothing at construction and is nearly impossible to add afterwards. Schools
still have physical education; nothing in adult life replaces it.

## Asia already did this

<KeyFigure value="77%" label="of Singapore's residents lived in flats built by the Housing and Development Board in 2023, most of them owning the flat they live in" source="Statista, 2024" href="https://www.statista.com/statistics/966747/population-living-in-public-housing-singapore/" />

Singapore is the case everyone knows: a state agency built the housing stock of
a country. Malaysia is the example I keep coming back to, and here the checkable
and the seen have to be separated.

What the record shows: new homes launched in Kuala Lumpur and the Klang Valley
average [around 827 square
feet](https://www.edgeprop.my/content/1471152/five-things-you-probably-did-not-know-about-size-malaysian-homes),
mostly high-rise, while Malaysian condominiums commonly run [100 to 120 square
metres with three bedrooms](https://www.teoalida.com/world/malaysia/), and
larger units exist in quantity.

What I saw: they built those towers while labour was cheap, and they are going
to be glad of it when they are old. The flats are large and pleasant, the cities
are dense, everything is close. The country has obvious faults — it is not a
place you walk, the pavements stop and start, you get about on a scooter. But
pavements can be rebuilt later, once a city learns to run itself. Towers cannot
be built later, not easily and not cheaply. They put the expensive, irreversible
thing in first and left the cheap, fixable thing for afterwards. That ordering
is correct, and we have it backwards.

<ObjectionList title="The objections, which are good ones" intro="The four the research behind this chapter found strongest. The answers are offered; where a number was missing it has not been invented.">
  <Objection claim="Who pays?" verdict="Unanswered until someone costs it on real land.">
    Land, rail and buildings, at scale, up front. The number is not in this
    chapter and will not be invented. What can be said about the shape: buying
    the field before it is a town is the cheapest moment to buy anything, and
    the rise in its value afterwards is created by the public decision to build
    there. Whether that uplift can fund the works is the question that decides
    whether this is a plan or a wish.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="People do not want towers." verdict="A convenient answer; build some and see.">
    Survey after survey finds Europeans saying they want a house with a garden.
    Part of the answer is that the choice on offer today is a house far out or a
    small flat in town, and a large flat in a well-served dense district has
    rarely been one of the options. That is a convenient answer, and the way to
    test it is to build some and see who moves in and who leaves.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Europe did this before, and it went badly." verdict="It went both ways, and the height was never the variable.">
    Britain built [32 new
    towns](https://www.tcpa.org.uk/resources/explore-the-uks-new-towns/) between
    1946 and the 1970s, now home to about 2.8 million people: not a catastrophe,
    not loved, criticised as paternalism from the first week, with rents that
    excluded many of the poorest. France's *grands ensembles* went far worse —
    built fast, left without services or transport, now [synonymous with poverty
    and exclusion](https://metropolitiques.eu/Grands-Ensembles-Retracing-a.html),
    many demolished. Vienna is the counter-case: the city has been the landlord
    for a century and [roughly 60% of
    residents](https://socialhousing.wien/policy/the-vienna-model) live in
    municipal or subsidised housing without any of it being a byword for
    failure. The common failure is building the housing and not building
    everything else — which is why the tram goes in on day one.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="A mistake in a standard is a mistake repeated ten thousand times." verdict="The risk to take most seriously.">
    A mistake in a single block is a bad block. A mistake in a standard is
    repeated in concrete for eighty years. Cheap construction, bad management,
    one monotonous design, one income group in one district — every one of
    those was a real failure mode last time.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

<EvidenceBox>
  Not an essay. Two or three districts under these rules — minimum heights,
  large flats with unheated workshop space, rail before occupancy, a gym in
  every building, allotments at the edge — in different countries, with
  different builders and tenure models, and the cost and the occupancy
  published. Then ten years of the boring measurements: who leaves, what it
  costs to maintain, how far children get outdoors, what happens to the price
  of everything around it. If the districts empty out, the chapter is wrong,
  and it will be visible.
</EvidenceBox>

I would rather we build this while it is still cheap to build, and argue about
the details afterwards, than have the argument perfectly and build nothing. The
towers cannot be added later. The pavements can.

<SourceList items={[
  { title: "Effect of time spent outdoors at school on the development of myopia among children in China", url: "https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.10803", note: "JAMA, 2015 — the Guangzhou randomised trial" },
  { title: "Interventions to slow progression of myopia in children", url: "https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD013549.pub2/abstract", note: "Cochrane review" },
  { title: "Overcrowding rate in the EU", url: "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/w/ddn-20251222-1", note: "Eurostat news, 2025 — 2024 data" },
  { title: "Share of the resident population living in HDB flats, Singapore", url: "https://www.statista.com/statistics/966747/population-living-in-public-housing-singapore/", note: "Statista" },
  { title: "Five things you probably did not know about the size of Malaysian homes", url: "https://www.edgeprop.my/content/1471152/five-things-you-probably-did-not-know-about-size-malaysian-homes", note: "EdgeProp Malaysia" },
  { title: "Malaysia: housing and apartment sizes", url: "https://www.teoalida.com/world/malaysia/", note: "Teoalida" },
  { title: "Allotment gardens in Poland", url: "https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/10/11/3829", note: "Sustainability (MDPI), 2018" },
  { title: "150 years of the Public Health Act", url: "https://www.cieh.org/about-us/history-of-cieh/150-years-of-public-health-act/", note: "Chartered Institute of Environmental Health" },
  { title: "Explore the UK's new towns", url: "https://www.tcpa.org.uk/resources/explore-the-uks-new-towns/", note: "Town and Country Planning Association" },
  { title: "Grands ensembles: retracing a history", url: "https://metropolitiques.eu/Grands-Ensembles-Retracing-a.html", note: "Métropolitiques" },
  { title: "The Vienna model", url: "https://socialhousing.wien/policy/the-vienna-model", note: "Wiener Wohnen" },
]} />

<ProvenanceNote
  source="2026-09-25-redesigning-the-state-dump.md:143-182"
  dictated={[
    "New towns in a field on new rules — an anti-capitalist idea, capital drains rent; the state buys the land or has it, or sells it under new rules; districts of towers or ten-storey blocks beside existing cities, with a minimum not a maximum; metro or tram at once (:145-151)",
    "Large flats, 80 to 200 square metres; a workshop part unheated or lightly heated; a terrace; space is the value; we did not grow up in a cave; 'eyes go bad because we look close, podobno'; build high so as not to sprawl (:153-159)",
    "Singapore and Malaysia; Malaysia built the towers while labour was cheap; not walkable, scooters; pavements later, towers cannot be built later; above N floors mandatory; no third land (:161-169)",
    "Allotment gardens as a Polish institution to recommend (:171-172)",
    "A gym in every building, possibly around the clock, with a view into the distance; a new standard as at the industrial revolution — what a person must be given for family, school and medicine to work; prevention; PE stays (:174-182)",
  ]}
  added={[
    "The Public Health Act 1875 as the dated form of 'the standard set at the industrial revolution' — proposed",
    "The Guangzhou trial and the Cochrane review behind his 'podobno' — proposed (ASK-1)",
    "Eurostat overcrowding, Singapore's HDB share, Malaysian flat sizes, allotment hectares — sourced figures, proposed",
    "The four objections, the British new towns, the grands ensembles and Vienna — proposed",
    "The comparison table of 1875 against the standard due — an arrangement of his list, proposed",
  ]}
  cut={[

# Who It Earns For

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/who-it-earns-for


import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';
import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: the shortage is physical, not monetary, so the only question left is who the machines earn for. */}

You can print as much money as you like. It will not make a nurse appear.

That sentence is the floor under everything else on this site.
[The pension argument](/book/designing-our-retirement) ends with a demand for
work that will not be there; this chapter is about what has to be true of the
thing we build so that the work is there, and so that the benefit of it reaches
the people who paid for it.

## Money cannot buy a service nobody supplies

We talk about the demographic crisis as if it were a funding problem. A funding
problem has a monetary answer: raise contributions, cut benefits, shift the
retirement age, borrow. Every one of those answers moves claims around. None of
them creates the thing being claimed.

When there are too few working-age people, the shortage is physical. Somebody
has to wash an eighty-year-old, drive the bus, harvest the field, answer the
phone at the clinic at two in the morning.

<Callout kind="claim">
  If nobody does it, the service does not become expensive. It stops existing.
  You stand at the counter with a full account and there is nobody behind it.
</Callout>

So the task is not to fund the future. It is to design the market that will
supply it, care, food, transport, public services, with far fewer hands than we
have now. If we do not design it, no amount of money will conjure it. We can
print until the presses wear out and it changes nothing. That is also why this
is an engineering project with a political wrapper, rather than a political
project with an engineering appendix.

## It has to produce a surplus

A system that only feeds itself is not enough.

Whatever we build, automated municipal services, autonomous farming and
logistics, machines in care, has to earn more than it costs to run. It has to
keep the people who work on it, and then have something left over. That
leftover is the whole point. It is what pays for the services the rest of us
live on without working for them: children, the old, the sick, and everyone
between jobs. Every productive economy has done this; we are going to ask it of
a smaller number of people and a larger number of machines, which means the
surplus has to be designed in rather than hoped for.

## School meals, and why they are the example

Here is the worked case I keep coming back to.

An automated food chain, growing, processing, moving, that is genuinely cheap
can feed every child in every school in the country, free, or so close to free
that the price stops being a question anyone asks. Not as charity. As a normal
output of capacity that exists anyway. That is how the technology gets popular.

Right now, when an ordinary person hears "robots", they hear "my job". They are
not being stupid; that is the version they have been shown. The argument that
automation is good for them is abstract, and abstract arguments lose. A hot meal
their child eats every day, for free, produced by the thing everyone is arguing
about, is not abstract. It is the difference between a technology people
tolerate and a technology people defend. If the first visible thing automation
does in a town is feed its children, the politics of the next twenty years look
very different from the politics we get if the first visible thing it does is
empty a warehouse.

So deploy it where people see it, and where the benefit is unmistakably theirs.
Municipal services first, as
[the robotics chapter](/book/robotic-reindustrialisation) argues, and food on
the table of somebody who did not have to pay for it.

## It has to earn for society, not only for capital

Now the part that decides whether any of this was worth doing.

The machines will earn. The question is whose account the earnings land in.
This technology has to pay for itself, and it has to pay not the owners of
capital but us; it has to earn for society. If automation replaces the labour
our pensions depend on and the returns flow to whoever owns the fleet, we will
have solved production and destroyed the distribution that made solving it
worthwhile. A continent full of robots and empty of purchasing power has not
fixed its demographic problem; it has changed the shape of it.

<SideNote label="Argued in full">
  Cheap before owned, open standards, hard to monopolise: the design goal is in
  [Cheap Is Wealth](/book/cheap-is-wealth); the rule that every proposal must
  answer it is at [Who captures the gains](/vision#who-captures-the-gains).
</SideNote>

Cheapness and open standards are the best defence we have, and they are not a
guarantee. "It must earn for society" is easy to say and easy to mean nothing
by. Three tests, proposed here, for what it would mean in practice:

- **Public buyers get the output, not just the invoice.** When a municipality or
  a pension system funds capacity, what it gets back is the service, meals,
  cleaning, transport, care hours, not a financial return it then spends buying
  the same service back at whatever price the owner sets.
- **Pension contributions buy the thing they were meant to buy.** Money set
  aside for our old age, invested in the machines that will care for us, is the
  one investment that delivers the service directly rather than a claim on
  somebody else's.
- **The surplus is visible and named.** A system whose surplus nobody can point
  to will be quietly captured. Whoever runs it should have to say, in public and
  in numbers, what it produced and where that went.

## Direct democracy is the instrument

Something has to keep making the decision, year after year, in our favour. That
something is us, and this is what direct democracy is also for: so that the
benefits of the technology are ours.

A body of a few hundred people can be lobbied into handing a public asset to
whoever asks nicely and pays well. It is cheap to do and it has been done,
repeatedly, to things we built together. Decisions taken by everyone are not
incorruptible, but they are far more expensive to corrupt. The choices this
chapter is about, what the surplus is spent on, who may own the fleet that does
public work, whether school meals are free, are simple to state, they affect
everybody, and people have real opinions about them. That is the profile of a
question that belongs to a
[citizens' vote](/book/direct-democracy#the-words-in-one-place) rather than to
a committee.

## Is this communism?

I want to deal with this myself rather than wait for someone to say it.

This was, in part, what communism was about. Only in communism the point was to
give power to the party, so that the party would take the technology and divide
it among the people. I think the power should go to the people, and to a system
that balances itself. Then, perhaps, a better world can be built.

So what I am saying is probably mildly communist, in that sense. Though it may
not be the right word; I would look for a better one, and I understand what is
meant by it. I assume the state can build a better world through intervention.
But I am also for the free market, in the way China does it, in the way they
[steer](/book/steering#what-to-learn-from-china-stated-carefully).

{/* ASK-1 (surplus-and-steering-dump.md:26-34): this is your own framing, kept once, here, as the editorial default of 2026-09-25 (R4 Q1). cheap-is-wealth carries a second, sharper verdict ("in effect communist"); it should shrink to a link here. Confirm the framing, or give the better word you said you would look for. */}

## Words that fit better

Three terms were offered to me while this chapter was being edited, as words
that describe parts of the position more precisely than the one above. I have
not chosen one. They are set out here because they are useful, with their
sources, not because any of them is yet mine.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="Three offered terms, and what each would name here"
  columns={[
    { label: "Predistribution", kind: "proposed" },
    { label: "Citizens' wealth fund", kind: "proposed" },
    { label: "Social market economy", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "What it names", cells: ["Shaping who earns and owns before tax and transfers, rather than correcting afterwards", "A public fund that holds a national asset and pays society from it", "A competitive market bound to social progress, in the Union's own founding text"] },
    { dimension: "Where it comes from", cells: ["Jacob Hacker, political scientist, 2011", "Norway's Government Pension Fund Global; Alaska's Permanent Fund", "Article 3(3) TEU, wording added by the Lisbon Treaty"] },
    { dimension: "What it would cover here", cells: ["The method: cheap open machines, public capacity, who owns the fleet", "One possible instrument for holding automated capacity", "The constitutional ground the demand could stand on"] },
    { dimension: "Status", cells: ["Offered, not adopted", "Offered, not adopted", "Offered, not adopted"] },
  ]}
  source="Equitable Growth explainer on predistribution; Hacker in the New Statesman (2013); NBIM; Alaska Permanent Fund Corporation; Article 3 TEU on EUR-Lex"
/>

**Predistribution.** Coined by the political scientist Jacob Hacker, it means
shaping how income and assets are distributed before tax and transfers, rather
than letting the market produce an outcome and correcting it afterwards with
benefits: raising wages rather than topping them up, changing who owns a thing
rather than taxing what it earns
([Equitable Growth](https://equitablegrowth.org/predistribution/);
[Hacker's argument](https://www.newstatesman.com/politics/2013/07/meet-mr-predistribution-jacob-hacker)).
Most of what this site proposes is predistributive in that sense: it decides
the outcome upstream instead of arguing about compensation downstream.

**A citizens' wealth fund.** Norway put its petroleum revenue into the
Government Pension Fund Global and draws on it to support the state budget
([NBIM](https://www.nbim.no/)). Alaska did something different with the same
idea: the Alaska Permanent Fund pays an annual cash dividend to every resident
([Alaska Permanent Fund Corporation](https://apfc.org/)). The open question for
us is whether automated productive capacity can be held the same way, and
whether the model survives when the asset is a fleet of machines that
depreciates rather than oil that sits in the ground. What I asked for is
services, school meals first. A cash dividend is an option that has been offered
alongside, not the demand.

**The social market economy.** Article 3 of the Treaty on European Union
commits the Union to "a highly competitive social market economy, aiming at full
employment and social progress", language added by the Lisbon Treaty
([Article 3 TEU](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX%3A12008M003)).
A market that produces, with an obligation that its gains reach society, is a
fair description of what this chapter asks for, and it is written into the
founding text of the thing being asked. That is worth knowing before anyone
calls the idea foreign to Europe.

{/* ASK-2 (surplus-and-steering-dump.md:88-91): the three terms were the editor's offer, "he decides". Adopt any of them as your vocabulary, or leave all three marked as offered? */}

<EvidenceBox title="What would settle the open parts">

Whether automated public provision produces a surplus at all, and how big: a
real municipal deployment with published costs and outputs over a budget cycle.
Whether public services change how people feel about automation, the
load-bearing claim in the middle of this chapter: feed children in one region
and measure opinion there against a region where the first visible robot took a
job. Whether a fund model works when the asset depreciates: somebody with the
right training can model it, and the answer changes how the instrument should
be designed. The legal questions, public ownership of productive capacity,
pension money in public infrastructure, procurement written to keep suppliers
cheap and interoperable, join the list in
[The Political Path](/book/political-path).

</EvidenceBox>

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "Publish what it cost and what it produced. A surplus nobody can point to will be quietly captured.",
  "Keep the interfaces open, so the next town can run it without asking permission.",
  "Deploy where the benefit is obvious to people who did not fund it, and let them see it working before anyone asks them to vote on it.",
]}>
  If you are building any of this, build it so the surplus is visible. That is
  a design instruction, not a sentiment.
</MeansForYou>

<ProvenanceNote
  source="2026-09-25-surplus-and-steering-dump.md:10-34 (money cannot buy absent services; the surplus; school meals; earn for society; his own placing against communism)"
  dictated={[
    "If nobody works on the labour market and we do not design the market that will supply the services, no money will make them appear; we can print and nothing comes of it (:12-14)",
    "The system must generate a surplus and keep those who work on it; public services such as free or very cheap school meals, to popularise the technology (:16-19)",
    "The technology must pay for itself and pay not the owners of capital but society; direct democracy is also for keeping the benefits ours (:19-22)",
    "Communism gave the power to the party to take and divide the technology; he wants the power with the people and a system that balances itself; 'probably mildly communist in this sense, though maybe not the right word; I would look for a better one'; state intervention can build a better world; also free-market, in the way China steers (:26-34)",
  ]}
  added={[
    "The three tests for 'earns for society' (output not invoice, pensions buy the service, surplus visible and named): proposed",
    "'When an ordinary person hears robots they hear my job' and the tolerate/defend distinction: editorial elaboration of 'spopularyzować tę technologię' (:19), no first person",
    "Predistribution, citizens' wealth fund, social market economy: offered terms with sources (the dump's agent reading :86-89), proposed, not adopted (ASK-2); a cash dividend named as an offered option, not his demand",
    "The evidence box and the closing instructions: proposed",
  ]}
  cut={[
    "Four restatements of the opening sentence in the first two sections: compressed to two",
    "The paragraph re-summarising the ownership argument from two other chapters and then declining to relitigate it: replaced by two sentences and a side note (one argument, one home)",

    "The Norway fund's size in dollars: no primary figure checked; removed",
  ]}
  open={["ASK-1", "ASK-2"]}
/>
