# Cheap Is Wealth

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/cheap-is-wealth


import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import PullQuote from '../../../components/PullQuote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: wealth is low prices, so scale and open standards are the distribution mechanism. */}

Wealth is when things are cheap, not when they are expensive. When something is
expensive, nobody can afford it and the people who supply it take the gain.
When it is cheap, you can buy it, and everybody ends up better off: the people
at the bottom live well, and the people above them live better still.

That sentence sounds obvious and almost nothing in our industrial policy acts on
it. We subsidise producers, protect margins, and count success in the size of a
sector rather than in the price its customers pay. I want to turn that around.
**Making things cheap is the goal, not a side effect of chasing some other
goal.** European transport has to be cheap and automated. If the machines
arrive and prices stay where they are, we built them for somebody else.

[Who It Earns For](/book/who-it-earns-for) argues that the system we build must
produce a surplus that reaches society. This chapter is the other half: the
surplus reaches people mostly through the price, and the price is decided by
whether we deploy at scale or keep the thing rare.

## Rare means they win, cheap means we win

Take any new capability and follow it two ways.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="The same invention, two ways"
  columns={[
    { label: "Kept rare" },
    { label: "Pushed to mass scale" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "Who sets the price", cells: ["A handful of suppliers", "Nobody; volume does"] },
    { dimension: "Where the value lands", cells: ["Their balance sheet", "Everyone who buys it"] },
    { dimension: "What you keep", cells: ["The right to read about it", "The difference between what it cost and what it costs now"] },
    { dimension: "What it is called", cells: ["A luxury", "Unremarkable"] },
  ]}
/>

Wealth in a society is mostly that accumulated difference — the long list of
things that used to be a luxury and are now unremarkable. When it goes the other
way, that is not a moral failure by anybody; it is what scarcity does. So
"democratising the benefits of technology" is not a slogan about ownership
papers. In the first instance it is a decision about volume and price. Build
for scale, keep the standards open, refuse to let the thing be enclosed, and the
distribution happens through the till.

<SideNote label="Applied to machines">
  The same rule for robots — cheap, open, hard to monopolise — in [Robotic
  Reindustrialisation](/book/robotic-reindustrialisation#cheap-beats-owned).
</SideNote>

## Technological unemployment: build what we never offered

A lot of people are going to lose work to AI. I am not going to pretend
otherwise.

But I am a positivist about the technological sciences, and I mean something
specific by it. **Do not put the effort into how work is being taken away. Put
it into producing value we never offered before.** That is where the employment
is. So the policy question is not "how do we protect this occupation". It is
"what could people have, that they cannot have today at any sane price, and
what would it take to deliver it at scale". Search for that. Fund the search.
That is a better use of a ministry than another retraining scheme aimed at the
jobs that are leaving.

## A worked example I am building myself

I built an application that generates made-to-measure furniture through a chat.
You describe what you want, it designs it, and you order it online.
Made-to-measure furniture has always been rare and expensive: hard to find
someone good, hard to explain what you wanted, and the design work cost more
than the wood. Most people gave up and bought a box that nearly fitted.

I expect the startup to create **more** work for the people who assemble
furniture, not less. Once the design step is nearly free, made-to-measure stops
being a luxury and becomes an ordinary thing to order, and there will be far
more orders than there ever were. The value could not be delivered at scale
before. That is the pattern: a cheap thing that did not exist, paid for by
volume, with hands needed at the end of it.

I should say the other half, because it is true. **This is also the uberisation
of work.** The fitter becomes a contractor taking jobs off a platform, and the
platform holds the customer relationship, the pricing and the ratings. Both
things are happening at once: more work, on worse terms, unless we decide the
terms.

<PullQuote>Wealth is when things are cheap, not when they are expensive.</PullQuote>

## Share the gains from capital, and start now

A technological revolution is when the division of the gains gets decided. It
gets decided early, quietly, by whoever is in the room, and then it holds for a
generation. We are in that room now, which is why this belongs in a political
programme rather than in a paper about the future of work.

What I want is not one new ownership law. It is **experiments in how people
organise, funded properly**: cooperatives, mutuals, employee-owned firms,
private capital, and mixed forms nobody has tried yet. Give them support and
grants, let most of them fail, and look at what the survivors do to prices and
to the people who work in them.

I think it is unfair that we subsidise private capital so heavily and put
almost nothing into cooperative forms. That is my claim, not a finding: the
research behind this chapter found no clean euro-for-euro comparison of public
support to cooperatives against public support to private firms in the EU, and
none is invented here. What is documented is narrower and points the same way.
The Commission's own [study on state aid and access to finance for social
enterprises](https://employment-social-affairs.ec.europa.eu/study-state-aid-access-finance-social-enterprises-and-recruitment-disadvantaged-workers-form-wage_en)
finds that the rules — age limits on eligible firms, the requirement to match
public money with private investment — create hurdles for social-economy
enterprises, that they lean on small *de minimis* schemes which cap their
growth, and that national authorities often avoid state-aid routes because the
rules are complex. A rule that pays out in proportion to the private investment
you can attract is a rule written for firms with shareholders; a cooperative
does not have them, by construction.

<EvidenceBox>
  Total public support — grants, tax expenditure, guarantees, subsidised credit
  — per euro of turnover and per employee, split by legal form, across a few
  member states. If the numbers show no tilt, the claim above goes. Until
  somebody runs them, it is the author's argument and not a finding.
</EvidenceBox>

The obvious question — is this communism? — gets one answer on this site, in
[Who It Earns For](/book/who-it-earns-for#is-this-communism), and it is not
repeated here.

## Write the proposal

[The Shorter Week](/book/the-shorter-week) is the other answer to the same
pressure: take the productivity as time rather than as unemployment. This
chapter is the first answer — take it as cheapness, and keep hunting for the
value nobody has been able to deliver yet. They are not alternatives. Fewer
hours only feel like freedom if the things you buy with the rest of your life
are cheap.

I think a better vision is enough to take power honestly and democratically.
That is what an election is supposed to be: whoever has the better proposal for
the voters. Nobody has one for the decade we are walking into, which is an
opening, not a complaint. We have AI. We have time, because the work is ending.
So let us write the proposal.

<MeansForYou actions={[
  "Name one thing people cannot have today at any sane price, and what it would take to deliver it at scale. That is a proposal; a complaint about a sector is not.",
  "If you run a cooperative, a mutual or an employee-owned firm, publish what public support you received per employee. The comparison nobody has run starts with your number.",
]}>
  The question to ask of every machine, every subsidy and every industrial
  strategy is the same one: does the price fall?
</MeansForYou>

<ProvenanceNote
  source="2026-09-25-redesigning-the-state-dump.md:254-296"
  dictated={[
    "Technological unemployment: a positivist of the technological sciences — concentrate on value we never offered, not on how work is taken; that is where the employment is (:256-260)",
    "The made-to-measure furniture application; more work for the people who assemble; uberisation on one side, value that could not be delivered before on the other (:262-269)",
    "Wealth is when it is cheap; when it is expensive, capital benefits; European transport cheap and automated; democratise the benefits by delivering at scale (:273-278, :289-292)",
    "Experimental forms — cooperatives, private capital, with support; unfair that private capital is subsidised so much and cooperatives are not; share the gains from capital, now, because the revolution is now (:280-287)",
    "A better vision is enough to take power democratically and honestly; whoever has the better project for the voters; we have AI and time; write the proposal (:292-296)",
  ]}
  added={[
    "The rare-versus-scale table — an arrangement of his sentences, no new claim",
    "The Commission study on state aid to social enterprises and the reading of it — proposed",
    "The per-euro comparison in the evidence box — proposed",
  ]}
  cut={[
    "'To jest de facto komunistyczne, tylko że nie będziemy tego robić centralnym sterowaniem' (:280) — the communism question has one home, Who It Earns For (decision of 2026-09-25, Q1); this chapter links",
    "'Made-to-measure goods have to be cheap. Care hours have to be cheap.' — not dictated; only transport is (:277)",
    "The second full statement of rare-versus-cheap (R4) — folded into the table",
  ]}
/>

# Direct Democracy

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/direct-democracy

import Callout from '../../../components/Callout.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import Objection from '../../../components/Objection.astro';
import ObjectionList from '../../../components/ObjectionList.astro';
import Playbook from '../../../components/Playbook.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import PullQuote from '../../../components/PullQuote.astro';
import SideNote from '../../../components/SideNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: representative democracy is the wrong shape, and the highest-leverage demand is the Swiss instrument — binding, copied not invented, demanded across the whole Union at once. */}

We vote every four years. For twenty years it has got worse.

That is not a mood, it is a record. Start at the crash of 2008 and follow the
line: one crisis, then another, then a third, and at the end of it a continent
talking about war rather than about what it is going to build. Every few years
we were offered a new set of names and we took it, and the direction did not
change. Twenty years is enough evidence. Representative democracy is not
delivering for Europe, and it is not going to start next term.

I have been waiting for the election that turns this around since I started
writing about reform, and it has not come. At some point the honest conclusion
is that the problem is not which people we elect. It is the arrangement we
elect them into.

## Why it fails — the fair version

I do not know which of these weighs most. Four explanations, and they lead to
the same place:

- **Some of them may mean badly.** Possible, and unprovable at the scale people
  usually claim it.
- **Some of them cannot cope.** The problems are large, slow and technical; the
  job rewards speed, visibility and the next cycle.
- **A body of a few hundred people is an easy thing to manipulate or corrupt.**
  Wherever a country's decisions are taken by three hundred or six hundred
  identifiable individuals, influencing that country means influencing a few
  hundred people. That is a cheap, well-understood operation.
- **The capable people do not go.** In Poland a well-paid programmer earns more
  than the president, and does not have strangers throwing filth at him for a
  living. We built a selection mechanism and then act surprised by what it
  selects.

Whichever mix is true, the fix has to be structural. This system has failed us
and we need a new one.

## Where the lever is

If I am going to fight for something, I want it to be the thing that moves the
most.

Most political energy online goes into a loop: a government does something
foolish, we name it, we prove it is foolish although everyone already knows, we
build enough outrage to raise the cost, and next month it happens again. That
loop does not compound. So the question is not *what is wrong* but *where the
levers are*, and I find two.

**The first lever is direct democracy.** The ability to decide specific
questions ourselves, often, with a result that binds. It changes every other
fight at once, because it changes who has to be persuaded.

One piece of precision, once. What Switzerland has, and what I am proposing, is
**semi-direct democracy**: parliament and government carry on, and citizens
hold two instruments to intervene in their work — the **citizens' initiative**,
which proposes a change and forces a vote on it, and the **optional
referendum**, which strikes down a law parliament has passed. The accelerator
and the brake. I will go on saying "direct democracy" through the rest of this,
because it is the phrase everyone uses and it names the thing we are adding.

<SideNote label="Defined once">
  The two instruments, the Swiss numbers and the ask on this site are stated in
  one place, [at the end of this chapter](#the-words-in-one-place); every other
  chapter points there.
</SideNote>

**The second lever is English as a working language.** That one is economic —
the floor under a European digital economy, European media, European companies
whose capital is not French or German but simply European. [The floor
layer](/vision#language) makes that argument. Language is the economy's lever.
Direct democracy is the political one, and without it the rest is a wish list
handed to people who have not delivered for twenty years.

## It is also the democratic answer to the anger

I hear voices calling for aggression — against migrants, sometimes against
politicians. That anger is real and much of what caused it is real too. But
there are democratic ways to settle this, and if we do not put one of them in
front of people, the other kind of answer is what fills the space.

**Direct democracy is the democratic answer.** It takes the same anger and
points it at a mechanism instead of at a group of human beings. It gives a
person who feels ignored something to demand that is specific, legal and
winnable. Discontent with nothing to do becomes contempt; discontent with an
instrument becomes reform.

<ObjectionList title="The two objections I expect">
  <Objection claim="Nationalists will be the first to use the instrument." verdict="The fear of the next government is the case for the brake, not against it.">
    The globalists warn us about the nationalists, and they may be partly right;
    I am wary of those forces too. That is an argument *for* the instrument. A
    new party that happens to be nationalist is no guarantee that the nation's
    interest is served, and if representative democracy has failed once it can
    fail again in different colours. Direct democracy is what makes the change
    safe whoever wins the next election. It may even be that Europe has not
    swung harder because people fear those forces and have no other handle on
    their state. Give them the handle.
  </Objection>
  <Objection claim="Crowds vote terrible things into constitutions on a bad Tuesday." verdict="Answered at length in the safeguards chapter, including the fact that cuts against me.">
    History's record of mass harm is a record of what governments did, not what
    electorates voted for. And the Swiss model comes with its safety mechanisms
    attached — validity checks, a double majority, a counter-proposal on the same
    ballot. They are itemised in [The Safeguards We Copy Too](/book/safeguards),
    beside the strongest case against them.
  </Objection>
</ObjectionList>

## The playbook

So here is what I think we should do, in order. Three of the steps need more
than a line; they have their own sections below.

<Playbook steps={[
  { action: "Do not only demand that this or that policy stop.", why: "The wave passes and the machine is unchanged. On the wave of the anger, demand direct democracy itself; every scandal is an argument for it." },
  { action: "Treat this as the real dividing line.", why: "Not left against right: whether a person is willing to give power to people or not. Demanding it shows who is actually a democrat, because refusing to answer is an answer." },
  { action: "Demand it of everyone.", why: "Government and opposition, the ones you like and the ones you do not. Push and vote for whoever is for it, from any camp, and note who suddenly finds reasons the public cannot be trusted." },
  { action: "Paper referendums first, digital later.", why: "Paper works and nobody can dismiss it as a technology experiment. The digital layer is built beside it, as something we learn on, and paper stays as the fallback." },
  { action: "Decide every three months, not every four years.", why: "A mandate you cannot correct for four years is not control, it is a receipt. Frequent decisions on real questions turn an audience into a principal." },
  { action: "Copy the Swiss model. Do not get clever.", why: "A proven, European, documented model, adopted broadly rather than reinvented — binding votes, and the safeguards that come with them.", href: "#copy-the-swiss-model" },
  { action: "Demand it across the whole Union at once.", why: "One state reforming alone is a target. A continent reforming together is a fact.", href: "#the-whole-union-at-once" },
  { action: "Build something to vote for.", why: "A mechanism is not a programme. Technocratic movements across the Union, whose offer is real work rather than grievance.", href: "#build-something-to-vote-for" },
]} />

<PullQuote>A mandate you cannot correct for four years is not control, it is a receipt.</PullQuote>

## Copy the Swiss model

Switzerland has run binding citizen votes at federal, cantonal and communal
level for well over a century: the one large, long-running, working example of
a country where citizens routinely decide policy directly and the state still
functions. It has costs — turnout, money, slowness — and [the safeguards
chapter](/book/safeguards#what-the-swiss-model-costs) lists them. But it is
proven, it is European, and it is documented. **Adopt it broadly. Do not
reinvent it.** Every hour spent designing a novel mechanism is an hour not
spent demanding one that already runs.

Two things follow from copying rather than inventing. **The votes are
binding** — both instruments. A vote the government may read as advice is the
instrument we already have, and it is the one that failed. And **the thresholds
are shaped by Switzerland's**, scaled to our electorates and rounded: my figure
is **2% of the electorate to launch an initiative and 1% to force a
referendum**, stated once [below](#the-words-in-one-place), with the arithmetic
for Poland and the Union in [the safeguards
chapter](/book/safeguards#the-arithmetic-at-our-scale). Copying the model means
copying its safety mechanisms too; that chapter is the itemised list.

## The whole Union at once

This is the part people get wrong, and the cost of getting it wrong is
historical. We wrote the Constitution of the Third of May in 1791, the first
written constitution in Europe, and within four years Poland did not exist. A
single country that reforms itself into something better while its neighbours
do not is a country that gets rolled over. **One state reforming alone is a
target. A continent reforming together is a fact.**

So the demand is European from the first day — school councils, municipalities,
regions, national parliaments, the Union — everywhere at once, by peoples who
have understood that they have the same problem. Each country deploys its own
system; we build the systems together, as Europeans.

And the countries that do not want it? Then they do not want it, and nothing
happens to them. We aim at doing it together anyway, the way we should with a
common working language: by making it obviously worth joining. Doing it
together is part of the point. A demand made across the continent at the same
time is itself an act of European identity — Europeans changing something
together, by their own decision — and even a Europe of nations can own it,
because it takes nothing from any nation. It would show how much we already
have in common.

## Build something to vote for

A mechanism is not a programme. If we win the instrument and have nothing to
put through it, we will have replaced one kind of drift with another.

So the second half of the playbook is to build technocratic political
movements across the whole Union — patriotic and national as much as European,
because these are not opposites. Their offer is real work rather than
grievance: rebuild the Union digitally, on a common working language, with
digital administration, digital healthcare, digital courts and a serious
industrial programme in robotics. We have roughly thirty years of working
economy left to build it, and nobody currently in charge is building it. What
Central Europe can put in — software, digital democracy, administration and
courts, as an export — is argued in [The Total
State](/book/the-total-state#what-central-europe-puts-in).

## Elections do not stop

I am not proposing that we abolish parliaments or stop voting for governments.
We keep electing representatives and we keep having parties; that is what makes
this semi-direct. **Direct democracy is how citizens force things through in
between** — the initiative to push something on, the referendum to stop
something passing — and a correction mechanism changes how representatives
behave long before it is used, which is most of its value. If the
representatives will not deliver it, people demand it in the street until a
government that refuses it stands down. That sentence belongs on the page, not
between the lines.

A separate proposal on this site — [electing representatives by
portfolio](/book/choosing-people) — changes how they are chosen rather than
what citizens can do between elections. Whether it belongs inside this
programme is not settled here.

{/* ASK-1 (R4 Q10; direct-democracy-dump.md:239-242): is portfolio election (choosing-people) part of the direct-democracy programme, or a separate proposal? The chapter links it as separate until you say. */}

## Brexit, and what it proved

Consider what happened in Britain. An enormous social mobilisation, years of
argument, a vote to leave — and afterwards, immigration from elsewhere went up
rather than down. That was not democracy. It was a one-off vote, and citizens
went on not steering their state, which is why they are dissatisfied again with
the next thing it does. There is no continuous mechanism, and a single vote
every few years holds almost nothing.

## The Union of Nations

What I am proposing is a **Union of Nations**: nations get the tools to steer
themselves — real instruments, held by their own citizens, at every level from a
school council upward — and at the same time we integrate deeply where
integration actually pays, at the level of digital administration, of how our
states function as software.

The reason is economic. The economy we are walking into has few workers, and
the ones it has must be able to move — take a job in another member state
without losing their records, qualifications, healthcare history or pension.
That requires common digital plumbing. It does not require a nation to stop
being itself. And it is not a replacement for the Union we have: the Union of
Nations rebuilds the present Union from the inside. Nobody has to leave
anything, and nothing has to be dissolved first.

<EvidenceBox title="What I cannot settle, and what would">
  Two things. **Legal force:** what it takes for a binding citizen vote to have
  real effect at national and at Union level, and what the existing European
  Citizens' Initiative can and cannot do today — a lawyer's memo would settle
  it, and [the first move](/book/first-move) is built to find out. **Which
  questions:** where the boundary sits between what citizens decide directly and
  what needs people working on it full-time. My answer so far is Swiss practice:
  specialists prepare, citizens can intervene at any stage, and on the important
  questions they approve or reject. Where exactly that line falls is a study of
  the Swiss record, not a sentence from me.
</EvidenceBox>

## The words, in one place

These are the standard terms of the field, defined here once. The other
chapters and the glossary point back to this section rather than restating
them.

<Callout kind="definition" term="Semi-direct democracy" label="Definition · Semi-direct democracy">
  A system where parliament and government keep working as they do now, and
  citizens hold instruments to propose law and to overturn it. Switzerland's
  system, and what this site proposes.
</Callout>

<Callout kind="definition" term="Citizens' initiative" label="Definition · Citizens' initiative">
  Citizens collect signatures to propose a change and force a national vote on
  it, whether or not parliament wants one. In Switzerland: [100,000 signatures
  within 18 months](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/1999/404/en), for a
  change to the federal constitution. The ask on this site: 2% of the
  electorate, the author's figure. The accelerator.
</Callout>

<Callout kind="definition" term="Optional referendum" label="Definition · Optional referendum">
  Citizens collect signatures to put a law parliament has already passed to a
  national vote, which can strike it down. In Switzerland: [50,000 voters or
  eight cantons within 100 days](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/1999/404/en)
  of publication. The ask on this site: 1% of the electorate, the author's
  figure. The brake.
</Callout>

<Callout kind="definition" term="Unity of subject" label="Definition · Unity of subject">
  An initiative may not bundle unrelated matters together, and may not mix a
  general proposal with a specific draft. Breach it and the Federal Assembly
  declares the initiative invalid. It kills the rider — the popular thing
  carrying the unpopular thing through on its back.
</Callout>

{/* ASK-2 (2026-09-25-education-migration-workweek-dump.md:34): "38M czyli daj u nas 1 i 2 %" — 38 million is Poland's population; the registered electorate at the 2024 European election was 29.1 million (Eurostat's eligible-population estimate: 32.1 million). Two per cent of the electorate is about 582,000 signatures; two per cent of the population would be about 760,000. The safeguards arithmetic uses the electorate. Confirm the base. */}

The **double majority** (of voters and of cantons or states) and the **turnout
quorum** are defined where they do their work, in [the
safeguards](/book/safeguards#the-safeguards-one-by-one); the **European
Citizens' Initiative**, the Union's existing and non-binding instrument, in
[the first move](/book/first-move#how-it-actually-works).

## We are the sovereign

Underneath all of it is a claim of right, and I want to state it as a claim
rather than as a complaint. We are the sovereign. Not the parliament, not the
administration, not the governments that have failed us in one country after
another. The power is ours and it is lent. Given what the last twenty years
have produced, taking more of it back is not a radical act. It is the ordinary
response of an owner who has watched a manager underperform for two decades.

<MeansForYou actions={["The next time something the state does makes you angry, do not demand the reversal. Demand the instrument — binding, Swiss, at every level — and say so wherever you were going to complain.", "Ask every politician you can reach one question: will you give this power to people? Their answer sorts them faster than any manifesto."]}>
  The playbook above needs no permission and no organisation to start. It
  starts with the next thing that makes you angry.
</MeansForYou>

# The Safeguards We Copy Too

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/safeguards

import ComparisonTable from '../../../components/ComparisonTable.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import KeyFigure from '../../../components/KeyFigure.astro';
import MeansForYou from '../../../components/MeansForYou.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';
import SourceList from '../../../components/SourceList.astro';

{/* SPINE: copying the instrument means copying its safety mechanisms — and saying which of them are Swiss fact, which are a proposed mapping, and which are the author's own choices. */}

I have argued that we should copy the Swiss model of direct democracy and not
get clever about it. The objection people put first is what stops a crowd from
voting something terrible into the constitution on a bad Tuesday. The answer is
that Switzerland has thought about this for well over a century, and the model
comes with its safety mechanisms attached. **We are not buying only the
referendum. We are buying the safeguards too.**

One thing has to be said before the list. The author did not know the Swiss
safeguards and asked for them to be mapped — *"I do not know them, but you can
propose how to map them and set out what it would look like mapped"*. This
chapter is that mapping. The Swiss column is fact, sourced to the Federal
Constitution and the Federal Chancellery. The European and Polish columns are a
proposal made at his request and not yet adopted. His own choices — the votes
bind, two per cent and one per cent, paper as the permanent fallback,
specialists prepare and citizens approve — are marked as his where they appear.

## What we are copying

The two instruments — the citizens' initiative and the optional referendum — and
the ask of 2% and 1% are defined once, in [Direct
Democracy](/book/direct-democracy#the-words-in-one-place). This chapter assumes
them and adds the third Swiss instrument only where it matters: the mandatory
referendum, a vote that happens automatically because the subject requires it —
every change to the federal constitution, and accession to a supranational
community or a collective-security organisation (Art. 140).

The Swiss electorate is called [about four times a
year](https://www.aboutswitzerland.eda.admin.ch/en/direct-democracy) to vote on
an average of fifteen questions, and turnout in recent decades has been a
little over 40% on average. The instrument is used constantly and passes
rarely; both halves of that sentence matter.

<KeyFigure value="22 of 192" label="federal popular initiatives adopted, of those put to the vote between 1893 and 2014" source="Wikipedia, Popular initiative in Switzerland (Federal Chancellery data)" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_initiative_in_Switzerland" />

## The safeguards, one by one

Eight mechanisms. The table is the summary; the notes beneath it carry the
mechanics where the mechanics decide something.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="Eight Swiss safeguards and their proposed equivalents"
  columns={[
    { label: "Switzerland", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "Union", kind: "proposed" },
    { label: "Poland", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "1. Double majority", cells: ["People and cantons, for constitutional change (Art. 142)", "Votes cast and 14 of 27 member states, for treaty-rank change", "National majority and 9 of 16 voivodeships — the weakest mapping"] },
    { dimension: "2. Unity of subject and form", cells: ["Federal Assembly voids a bundled initiative (Art. 139)", "Copy; Court of Justice rules on referral", "Copy; Constitutional Tribunal rules"] },
    { dimension: "3. Validity against binding law", cells: ["Mandatory international law only (Art. 139)", "Non-derogable core of the ECHR — working default", "Same floor as the Union"] },
    { dimension: "4. Counter-proposal", cells: ["Parliament may put one on the same ballot (Art. 139)", "Copy unchanged", "Copy unchanged"] },
    { dimension: "5. Turnout quorum", cells: ["None; majority of votes cast (Art. 142)", "None", "Drop the Art. 125 rule; approval quorum only for constitutional rank"] },
    { dimension: "6. Binding force", cells: ["The result changes the law", "Automatic trigger, binding result", "Sejm must call the vote; result binds"] },
    { dimension: "7. Layers below the national", cells: ["Cantons and communes, lower thresholds", "Member states, regions, municipalities, schools", "Voivodeships, municipalities, schools"] },
    { dimension: "8. Fixed voting dates", cells: ["About four a year, questions bundled", "Fixed dates, bundled", "Fixed dates, bundled"] },
  ]}
  source="Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation, Art. 138–142; Constitution of the Republic of Poland, Art. 125; mapping proposed 2026-09-25, not adopted"
/>

### 1. The double majority, worked

A proposal put to the People *and the Cantons* passes only if a majority of
those voting approve it **and** a majority of the cantons approve it (Art. 142
§2). Each canton's vote is decided by the result inside that canton (§3), and
six cantons — Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell
Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden — carry half a cantonal vote each (§4).
With 20 full and 6 half votes that is 23 cantonal votes, so the threshold is
12. It protects the periphery from being outvoted by a dense core on the rules
themselves — the failure mode that ends federations.

Note the asymmetry, because it is the cleverest part of the design. The double
majority applies to constitutional change. The optional referendum — the
citizen veto on an ordinary law — needs only a majority of those who vote (Art.
142 §1). Vetoing is easy; amending the constitution is hard.

**The proposed Union equivalent** makes the member states the second chamber: a
citizens' vote on anything of treaty or constitutional rank passes only with a
majority of votes cast across the Union and a majority of member states, 14 of
27; a citizen veto of an ordinary legislative act needs only the popular
majority. The half-vote question is left open — the six Swiss half-cantons are
a historical artefact of cantons that split, not a formula anyone derived.
**The proposed Polish equivalent** is the weakest mapping in the set, and it
should be said rather than dressed up: Poland is not a federation, the nearest
unit is the voivodeship, and a constitutional-rank vote would need a national
majority plus a majority in 9 of 16 of them. The objection is real —
voivodeships are administrative, not constituent, and giving them a veto invents
a federalism Poland does not have.

{/* ASK-1 (answers-and-safeguards-dump.md:39-40): adopt the 14-of-27 and 9-of-16 double majorities as your position, or keep them as a proposal? A second chamber of voivodeships is a constitutional position with your name on it. */}

### 2 and 4. Validity, and the counter-proposal

An initiative that bundles unrelated matters, or mixes a general proposal with
a specific draft, is declared invalid by the Federal Assembly, in whole or in
part (Art. 139 §3). This kills the rider — the single most common way a
referendum is used to launder a decision the public did not actually approve.
The proposal is to copy it unchanged and say who rules: plausibly the Court of
Justice on referral in the Union, the Constitutional Tribunal in Poland. What
happens when the body ruling on validity is itself contested has no answer here
that survives a bad-faith government.

The Federal Assembly also recommends acceptance or rejection and may put a
**counter-proposal** beside the initiative; voters may say yes to both and
answer a third question on which they prefer (Art. 139 §5). That is the answer
to "referendums force a complicated question into yes or no": the expert body
puts a better-drafted version on the same ballot paper. It is also the shape I
actually want from specialists. **Specialists prepare the work; citizens can
intervene at any stage, and on the important questions they approve or reject
it.** Not a menu of priced options handed to the public like a restaurant card —
that is not how a state is run, and I will not load the promise that heavily.
Copy the counter-proposal unchanged at both levels. It is the cheapest
safeguard on the list and the one most likely to be dropped for looking
complicated.

### 3. The rights floor

An initiative that infringes **mandatory provisions of international law** is
invalid (Art. 139 §3) — the bans on torture, slavery and genocide, the
non-derogable core usually called *jus cogens*. This is the safeguard aimed at
the scenario the objectors raise: a majority voting to do to a minority what no
majority may do.

The Swiss filter is narrow on purpose, and the Swiss electorate has passed
initiatives that ran into Convention obligations and argued about the conflict
afterwards. A European version has to decide in advance whether the whole
European Convention on Human Rights binds an initiative or only its
non-derogable core. The two are materially different systems. This draft takes
the narrow option as its working default — the non-derogable core, less rather
than more — because it is the one the Swiss model actually runs, and it leaves
the choice marked.

{/* ASK-2 (R4; PLAN default 2026-09-25 "non-derogable ECHR core only"): confirm the narrow floor as your position, or choose the whole Convention. The women's-suffrage record below is the fact that argues for a stronger floor than the Swiss one. */}

### 5. No turnout quorum, and the Polish clause

Switzerland has no turnout quorum: a proposal passes if a majority of those who
vote approve it (Art. 142 §1). That looks like a missing safeguard and is a
deliberate one. With a turnout quorum, the way to defeat a proposal is to tell
your side to stay home; abstention gets counted as a no, and a boycott beats an
argument. The Venice Commission's [Code of Good Practice on
Referendums](https://www.venice.coe.int/webforms/documents/default.aspx?pdffile=CDL-AD%282022%29015-e)
says exactly this: it advises against both a turnout quorum and an approval
quorum, and accepts an approval quorum or a special majority only for questions
of fundamental constitutional significance (III.7).

A Polish national referendum is binding only if **more than half of those
entitled to vote take part** ([Constitution, Art.
125](https://www.constituteproject.org/constitution/Poland_2009)). That single
clause is why Polish referendums keep producing nothing, and it is what lets a
parliament hold one and ignore it. The proposal: drop the turnout quorum, make
the result binding on the votes cast, and keep an approval quorum only for
constitutional-rank questions, on the Venice Commission's line. It is the most
consequential change on this page and the one that will be fought hardest.

### 6. Binding force, and where Poland's instrument stops

In Switzerland the result changes the law: an adopted initiative amends the
constitution; a successful referendum kills the act. Poland already has a
citizens' motion for a referendum — 500,000 citizens may petition for one
([Act on the national referendum, Art.
63](https://isap.sejm.gov.pl/isap.nsf/download.xsp/WDU20030570507/T/D20030507L.pdf)) —
but the Sejm is not obliged to call it, and no deadline compels it to decide.
The right is to ask. That is the whole difference between the two systems, and
it is the thing itself, not a detail of implementation.

My position is the binding one: **the referendum binds**, both instruments. The
proposal that follows from it is an automatic trigger: signatures verified,
question valid, vote scheduled, with no discretionary step between the citizens
and the ballot box.

### 7 and 8. The layers below, and fixed dates

Federal votes are the visible part of the Swiss system. Cantons and communes
run their own initiatives and referendums with lower thresholds, and a citizen
votes far more often on local matters than national ones: the system is trained
where the stakes are small and the feedback is fast. Ours is not, and that is
the level to start at — school councils, municipalities, regions, then the
state, then the Union, the order he gave. Start where a mistake is cheap. It is
also where **paper voting in schools and town halls** is obviously affordable:
if a school hall can hold a national election, it can hold a local vote, and
the number of people turning out for a municipal question is not large. If
digital voting is too expensive, the answer is to work on the cost of it, not
to drop the votes.

Four fixed voting dates a year, questions bundled onto them, is how the Swiss
keep the cost down and the temperature low: a question that loses can come
back, so no ballot is the last word forever. I asked for decisions every three
months; the Swiss calendar is the same rhythm with a name. Fixed dates, at every
level.

## The arithmetic at our scale

The thresholds are my figure: **2% of the electorate to launch an initiative, 1%
to force a referendum.** The Swiss numbers, as a share of their electorate, are
the comparison, and that share is the only way to compare countries of
different sizes. Switzerland had 5,611,289 registered voters at the [September
2024 federal vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Swiss_referendums); so
100,000 signatures is 1.78% of the electorate and 50,000 is 0.89%. The 2:1
ratio between proposing and vetoing is Swiss; the level is his. The reasons
offered for rounding up rather than copying the share — a round figure people
can repeat, and an instrument this powerful being slightly harder to reach than
the one it is copied from — are the editor's, not a position he has taken.

<ComparisonTable
  caption="Signature thresholds, scaled — derived from the 2% / 1% rule"
  columns={[
    { label: "Switzerland", kind: "fact" },
    { label: "Union", kind: "proposed" },
    { label: "Poland", kind: "proposed" },
  ]}
  rows={[
    { dimension: "Electorate", cells: ["5,611,289", "≈ 360,000,000", "29,098,155"] },
    { dimension: "Citizens' initiative", cells: ["100,000 (1.78%)", "≈ 7,200,000 (2%)", "≈ 580,000 (2%)"] },
    { dimension: "Optional referendum", cells: ["50,000 (0.89%)", "≈ 3,600,000 (1%)", "≈ 290,000 (1%)"] },
    { dimension: "Collection window, initiative", cells: ["18 months", "18 months", "18 months"] },
    { dimension: "Collection window, referendum", cells: ["100 days", "6 months", "100 days"] },
    { dimension: "Second-chamber majority", cells: ["12 of 23 cantonal votes", "14 of 27 states", "9 of 16 voivodeships"] },
  ]}
  numeric
  source="Swiss electorate: Federal Chancellery, vote of 22 September 2024; Poland: registered voters at the 2024 European election (PKW); Union: the European Parliament's 2024 figure, which varies by source and cut-off — the Union row is accurate to a few per cent. Derived figures rounded."
/>

Three remarks on that table. **The Polish initiative number lands close to the
threshold Poland already uses:** about 580,000 against the existing 500,000 for
a referendum motion. So the problem with the Polish instrument is not the
number; it is that the result does not bind and the Sejm does not have to act.
**The 100-day veto window does not survive translation to Union scale.** A
hundred days to collect three and a half million signatures across 27 states
and 24 languages is a different task from fifty thousand in a country the size
of Switzerland; six months is proposed here, with the cost stated — every month
added is a month of legal uncertainty for the act being challenged. **The
European Citizens' Initiative is not this and is not close.** One million
signatures from seven member states, and the Commission is not obliged to
propose anything; the Union built the collection machinery and attached it to
nothing. [The first move](/book/first-move#how-it-actually-works) is about
using it anyway.

{/* ASK-3 (R4 Q3; derived figures): the Union electorate could not be re-verified from a primary source for this draft (the European Parliament results site publishes turnout, not the electorate; Eurostat's dedicated collection gives a higher eligible-population figure). The Polish base is registered voters, 29,098,155; Eurostat's eligible-population estimate for Poland is 32,148,844, which would make two per cent about 643,000. Confirm the base and the six-month window. */}

## What the Swiss model costs

The model has costs, and a chapter that copies it owes the list.

**Turnout is low** — [a little over 40%](https://www.aboutswitzerland.eda.admin.ch/en/direct-democracy)
on average in recent decades. Read that as fatigue, or as citizens sensibly
skipping the questions they do not care about; both readings are honest. It
does mean a determined, organised minority of the whole electorate can carry a
federal vote. **Money works.** Campaigns can be funded, and frequent voting
multiplies the surface. This is the strongest practical criticism of the model,
and this chapter has no answer to it beyond disclosure rules stricter than the
Swiss ones. **It is slow.** A law can be stopped after parliament has passed
it; a constitutional change takes years. In a crisis that is a liability, which
is why the emergency-act provisions exist — and those are themselves subject to
a referendum if they run past a year.

<EvidenceBox variant="against" title="The case against me">
  Swiss women got the federal vote in [February
  1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_Switzerland). An
  all-male electorate had voted the question down in 1959, two to one, and took
  twelve more years to reverse itself; the first federal election women voted in
  was 31 October 1971, and the last canton, Appenzell Innerrhoden, gave women the
  cantonal vote only after a Federal Supreme Court judgment of 27 November 1990.
  If you want a case where a majority withheld a right from a minority through
  the direct instruments, it is right here, in the model I am proposing to copy.
  It argues for the rights floor in safeguard 3 being stronger than the Swiss
  one — not for abandoning the instrument that eventually, slowly, corrected it.
</EvidenceBox>

## Where I stand, and the argument against me

My position is this: **history's record of mass harm is overwhelmingly a record
of what governments did, not what electorates voted for.** The catastrophes of
the last century were organised by states, by administrations, by small numbers
of people holding a monopoly of decision. I am much less afraid of a crowd
making a bad call on a Tuesday than of a cabinet making one for thirty years
with no mechanism to stop it. That is why I want the safeguards attached to the
instrument rather than used as an excuse to refuse it — and it is also why the
instrument matters for the rest of this site: direct democracy is what keeps
[the gains from the machines](/book/who-it-earns-for) with society rather than
with whoever owns them.

The standard counter-argument is serious and belongs here at full strength.
**Majorities have voted to restrict minorities.** Referendums on minority
rights have a bad record in several countries, including Switzerland; a right
that requires fifty per cent plus one is not a right but a permission; and the Swiss
women's vote above is this exact objection, evidenced, inside the model I want.
That argument is not settled here in his favour. What can be claimed is
narrower: the objection is an argument about *which safeguards* and *how strong
a rights floor*, not an argument for leaving decisions where they are now. Both
sides want a limit on what a majority may do. The disagreement is over who is
more dangerous without one.

## Left open in this draft

- **The rights floor** — the whole Convention or only its non-derogable core
  (safeguard 3; ASK-2).
- **Who rules on validity**, and what happens when that body is itself captured
  (safeguard 2).
- **The second chamber for Poland** — voivodeships are the least bad unit named
  here and they are not good (ASK-1).
- **The veto window at Union scale** — six months is a guess, not a finding
  (ASK-3).
- **Campaign-finance rules**, which have to be stricter than the Swiss ones and
  are not drafted here.
- **Digital voting** — paper first, digital built in parallel as something we
  learn on, paper kept permanently as the fallback for the basic functions of
  the state; what has to be true of identity, verification and audit before a
  digital referendum binds is unanswered.
- **Whether a Union instrument needs treaty change**, or whether an automatic
  referral obligation could be attached to the existing Citizens' Initiative
  first — the lawyer's question that decides how soon any of this can start.

<MeansForYou actions={["Before you sign anything that promises referendums, ask which of the eight safeguards it names. A demand that lists them is serious; one that does not is the instrument we already have."]}>
  This chapter is a checklist as much as an argument.
</MeansForYou>

# Steering

URL: https://zentala.eu/book/steering


import KeyFigure from '../../../components/KeyFigure.astro';
import EvidenceBox from '../../../components/EvidenceBox.astro';
import Playbook from '../../../components/Playbook.astro';
import PullQuote from '../../../components/PullQuote.astro';
import ProvenanceNote from '../../../components/ProvenanceNote.astro';

{/* SPINE: ask of any reform how long it takes to find out it was wrong and what correcting it costs. */}

Watch anyone ride a bicycle. They are never upright. They lean left, correct,
lean right, correct, and the correcting never stops; that is what holds them up.
Stand the same bicycle still and it falls over in two seconds.

Balance is not walking in a straight line. It is leaning back, then forward,
and still moving ahead. You do not stop. You go forward, lean one way, lean the
other, and catch your balance. Keeping balance means being in motion and
catching the middle again and again, not standing in it, because the middle
cannot be held. A state that refuses to lean is not stable. It is stalled, and a
stalled bicycle is a falling bicycle.

## We do not fall because we are wrong. We fall because we are slow.

Here is the pattern, and once you see it you will see it everywhere.

A direction gets set. It is held for years, past the point where everyone
involved can see it is not working. Then it is reversed at enormous cost, after
the money is spent, after the factories have retooled, after the competitors
have taken the market. And often enough, the thing the public said at the start
turns out to be roughly what happens in the end.

Notice what is broken there. It is not that a mistake was made. Every system
that does anything makes mistakes. The failure is in how long it took to correct
one. The cost is not in the wrong turn; the cost is in the distance travelled
before the wheel moved.

## The cars

The clearest example we have is the car industry, and the dates are the
argument.

| When | What happened |
|---|---|
| March 2023 | The Union adopts [Regulation (EU) 2023/851](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/851/oj): new cars and vans sold from 2035 must emit no CO2, in effect the end of the combustion engine in new cars. Germany holds up the final vote for about a month and extracts a carve-out for e-fuels, [agreed in the last week before adoption](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2023/03/28/in-win-for-germany-eu-agrees-to-exempt-e-fuels-from-2035-ban-on-new-sales-of-combustion-en). |
| 2023–2025 | The industry spends against the announced direction. |
| December 2025 | The Commission proposes replacing the 100 % cut with 90 %, so plug-in hybrids, range extenders and combustion cars can go on being sold after 2035, the last tenth offset through EU-made low-carbon steel, e-fuels and biofuels ([Euronews, 16 December 2025](https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2025/12/16/eu-carmakers-to-comply-with-90-emissions-reduction-by-2035-as-full-combustion-engine-ban-s)). Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland and Slovakia had pressed for it, and the carmakers harder. |

<KeyFigure
  value="2 years, 9 months"
  label="from the Union adopting the 100 % rule for 2035 to the Commission proposing to soften it to 90 %; derived from the two dates in the table"
  source="Regulation (EU) 2023/851, adopted March 2023; Commission proposal of 16 December 2025 (Euronews)"
  href="https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2025/12/16/eu-carmakers-to-comply-with-90-emissions-reduction-by-2035-as-full-combustion-engine-ban-s"
  aside
/>

A law that has to be renegotiated in the last week before it passes is a law
that was never settled. One qualification, because accuracy matters more than
rhetoric: the December 2025 text is a proposal, not yet law. It still needs the
member state governments and the European Parliament, and the final version may
differ. If you read this later than it was written, check where it landed.

Everything else about the episode is on the record, and it is bad enough. We set
a direction, told an entire industry to spend against it, held it for nearly
three years, and then softened it so that European manufacturers would not go
under. That is not a policy. That is a swerve. It is an embarrassment in front of
the whole world, an embarrassment for the Union's administration, that it could
not carry the thing through, and the embarrassment is not that they changed
their mind. Changing your mind is the correct response to new information. It is
that it took this long and cost this much, and that in the end it came out the
way the citizens wanted from the start.

<EvidenceBox variant="against" title="What this chapter cannot show">

"The citizens were against it from the start" is my reading, not a measured
fact. No poll is quoted here and none will be invented. What can be said without
inventing anything: the reversal happened, it happened under pressure from
industry and national governments, and nobody asked the public directly whether
this was the transition they wanted, at that speed. What would settle it is a
polling series on the 2035 rule from 2022 to 2025, by member state, which
somebody may already hold.

</EvidenceBox>

And the cost was paid twice. Once by the companies that invested in the
direction we announced, and again by the ones that hesitated because they
suspected we would not hold it. Both bets turned out to be reasonable. That is
the real damage of a slow system: it stops being rational to trust it, and after
that nobody plans on anything it says.

## A controller must correct at least as fast as the thing it steers

There is a name for this problem, and it is older than the European Union. It
was offered to me while this chapter was being edited; I did not arrive at it
myself, and it is set out here as the nearest prior art, not as my claim.

Ross Ashby's **law of requisite variety** says that a controller must have at
least as much variety in its responses as the system it is trying to control
throws at it; the usual short form is that
[only variety can absorb variety](https://www.businessballs.com/strategy-innovation/ashbys-law-of-requisite-variety/).
Stafford Beer spent his career applying this to organisations and to states,
and built the
[Viable System Model](https://www.businessballs.com/strategy-innovation/viable-system-model-stafford-beer/)
around it.

The part that matters here is simple enough to say in ordinary words. A
steering system that corrects once every four years can only steer a world that
changes once every four years. Ours does not. Technology, energy prices, supply
chains and wars move faster than that, and a four-year loop against a six-month
world is not governance; it is hoping.

## Direct democracy is the faster loop

This is why [direct democracy](/book/direct-democracy#the-words-in-one-place)
is not a matter of taste for me. Those movements, the lean and the correction,
are what it is. We fall over because we walk too slowly: too slow to decide,
too slow to set a direction, and then we set one and back out of it, and that
costs us a great deal. The instrument is the correction mechanism.

Frequent votes on specific questions do two things at once. They make
corrections more often, and because they happen more often, they make each
correction smaller. A wheel you touch every few seconds needs a nudge. A wheel
you touch once every four years needs a yank, and a yank at speed is how you
come off. The Swiss hold federal popular votes
[three to four times a year](https://www.admin.ch/gov/en/start/federal-chancellery/tasks.html).
That is not, as people assume, a country in permanent crisis from constant
voting. It is a country whose steering never has to move very far, because it
never goes very long without moving.

<PullQuote>
  Speed is the point. Not participation for its own sake, not fairness in the
  abstract: error correction, fast enough to matter.
</PullQuote>

## The other loop: who talks to whom

Voting is the loop between citizens and the state. There is a second loop that
is just as broken, and it runs between the state and the people who build
things.

Entrepreneurs feel they cannot get through to the government with what they
need for growth: which rule is strangling a sector, which permit takes nine
months, what an investment decision is waiting on. And from the other side,
there is no agreement between entrepreneurs and everybody else about how they
should be taxed and how the burden should be divided. Each group suspects the
other of freeloading, and neither has a room to say so in.

What I want instead runs in both directions. Business sends someone to talk to
the state: not the state planting a spy in a firm, but the firm sending a person
to speak with the state. And the state sends someone to talk to business. So
that there is communication, so that information flows. The state has to move
further into a communicating role: a negotiator, or perhaps not even a
negotiator, a system of checks and balances.

## What to learn from China, stated carefully

I will say the uncomfortable part plainly, and then bound it.

I think we can learn a lot from China about running a state, and the thing I
want to learn is not the party. Not one-party rule, not the absence of a free
press, not what happens to people who become inconvenient. None of that is on
offer here and none of it is what I am pointing at. I want more power in the
hands of citizens, not less.

China has its group of representatives and it works well for them; we should
have a group of representatives too, only ours should be democratic. Theirs are,
in a sense, also democratic: the party is somewhat more like a mafia, and people
get cleaned out, but apart from that the representatives are relatively
democratic. The part worth taking is not how those people are chosen. It is the
question of where representatives come from, from which social classes, and what
they represent.

{/* ASK-1 (surplus-and-steering-dump.md:38-42): the China passage is kept as you said it, including "relatively democratic" and "somewhat like a mafia". It is carefully bounded and it will still be the passage people quote. Confirm you want it published in this form. */}

Our answer is almost entirely geography. You represent a district. That is a
real thing to represent, but it is one axis, and a modern economy has several.
Nobody in our parliaments sits there as the person the machine-tool sector sent,
or the care workers, or the small logistics firms, with a mandate from them and
a duty to report back. Those people exist in the building, but they arrive as
lobbyists, paid by whoever pays them, visible to nobody. The shape of the
question is one we have stopped asking, and we should ask it again in a
democratic form: elected, transparent, revocable, answerable to the people who
sent them. I do not have a designed mechanism to hand you.

## Except we already built it, and left it toothless

Here the research behind this chapter turned something up that I had not named:
Europe already has institutions of exactly this shape. They sit in our capitals,
and almost nobody can name them. What follows is what was found, offered with
its sources.

**The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC)** is a Union body of
representatives of employers, workers and civil society that gives opinions on
EU legislation; it has existed since the Treaty of Rome, and its opinions are
advisory, with no veto and no formal power to stop anything. In March 2026 the
European Court of Auditors reported that the Committee delivered 84 % of its
opinions on time in 2019–2024 and that neither it nor the Committee of the
Regions systematically measures whether an opinion changed the final law
([Special report 12/2026](https://www.eca.europa.eu/en/publications/SR-2026-12)).
If a body cannot tell you whether it changed anything, that is usually because
it did not.

**In Poland, the Rada Dialogu Społecznego**, the Council for Social Dialogue, is
the national forum where unions, employers and the government are supposed to
meet. The idea is right. The practice is the complaint from every side of the
table: draft laws never reach it, or reach it too late to matter; bills are
routed around it; government seats sit empty. Union and employer
representatives alike have described it as
[stuck, operating but producing no results and no shared vision](https://www.pulshr.pl/zwiazki-zawodowe/rada-dialogu-spolecznego-w-impasie-brakuje-efektow-i-wspolnej-wizji-dzialan,115185.html).

So the conclusion is not "Europe needs a new institution for this". It is worse
and more useful than that: the institution exists, and it has no teeth. We built
the channel and then made sure nothing has to come out of the other end. What
these bodies lack is consequence. Four things that would give them some, none of
which needs a treaty change, proposed here and not yet adopted as a demand:

<Playbook title="What would give the channel consequence" steps={[
  { action: "A duty to answer.", why: "If a draft law goes to these bodies and they object, the legislator publishes a reasoned reply before proceeding. Not obedience: a written answer, on the record, that a journalist can quote back later." },
  { action: "A duty to ask.", why: "A law touching a sector does not move without that sector's representatives having had a real chance to see it. Bypassing the council becomes a defect in the process, not a tactic." },
  { action: "Publication by default.", why: "Every meeting, every position, every name. Most of what lobbying buys is privacy." },
  { action: "Visible people.", why: "If a sector sends a representative, the public knows who they are and can read what they asked for. A lobbyist nobody can name is worth more to his employer than a representative everybody can." },
]} />

Whether that is best done by reforming the EESC and the national councils, or
by wiring the same duties into the ordinary legislative procedure, is open. A
body with decades of institutional memory and no power is a better starting
point than a new body with neither.

## Why the two loops need each other

The votes decide direction: what kind of country this is going to be, who the
gains go to, what we will not accept. The dialogue supplies information: what a
decision will actually do once it hits a factory, a ward, a haulage firm. A
state with fast votes and no information corrects quickly towards the wrong
place. A state with good information and no votes knows exactly what to do and
does what the best-connected interest wants instead, which is a fair description
of the car file. You need the speed and you need the sensors.

If you take one thing from this chapter, take the question. Of any proposed
reform, ask not only whether it points the right way but: when this turns out
to be partly wrong, how long will it take us to find out, and how expensive will
it be to correct? That question kills a lot of grand plans and rescues a lot of
modest ones. It is the reason this site argues for instruments rather than for
programmes, and the reason [The Total State](/book/the-total-state) insists that
the correction mechanism ships alongside the digital machinery rather than after
it. A state that can see everything and cannot be corrected is a fast bicycle
with no handlebars.

<ProvenanceNote
  source="2026-09-25-surplus-and-steering-dump.md:36-74 (China and representation; business–state communication; balance as movement; the electric-car reversal)"
  dictated={[
